1607: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage.
1608: Normal sudoku and killer sudoku rules apply. (ie In cages, cells must sum to the small clue given in the top left corner of the cage. Digits may not repeat within a cage.) Cells separated by a knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit.
1609: Normal sudoku rules apply. In addition, both marked diagonals must contain the digits 1 to 9. Clues outside the grid give the sum of the cells along the indicated diagonal. Digits can repeat along these diagonals.
1610: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue given in the top left of the cage. Digits may not repeat within cages. Clues outside the grid give the sum of the cells along the indicated diagonal. Digits can repeat along these diagonals.
1611: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages digits sum to the small clue in the top left corner. Digits cannot repeat in a cage. One of the digits, X, is always worth twice its normal value if it appears in a killer cage in the grid. The digit X needs to be determined.
1612: Normal sudoku rules apply. Outlined regions are cages, digits cannot repeat in these regions. The sum of the digits in a cage is called the "cage total". A white dot exists between all cages where the cage totals have a difference of 1. A black dot exists between all cages where the cage totals have a ratio of 2. Note that there is a negative constraint ie all of the possible dots have been given.
1613: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Outside clues indicate the sum of digits in snakes of length X where X is the first digit in the row/column. Snakes begin at the cell directly next to a clue and are 1 cell wide regions where digits cannot repeat. A snake cannot touch itself orthogonally and cannot branch in 2 directions. No cell can be a part of more than 1 snake.
1614: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. Clues outside the grid give the sum of the digits along the indicated diagonal. Digits can repeat along these diagonals (unless they repeat in one of the 3x3 boxes).
1615: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered with fog. Placing correct digits will reveal the fog around that digit. Guessing is not required! A digit in a red circle indicates exactly how many red circles contain that digit. Additionally, a digit in a red circle must reappear at least once in its 8 surrounding cells. The two given circles contain the same digit. Digits along a purple arrow sum to the value in the attached circle. Red circles may or may not have arrows attached. Arrows do not share cells and do not cross.
1616: Normal sudoku rules apply. The purple line is an entropic line. Any set of three sequential cells along an entropic line must contain a low digit (1,2,3), a middle digit (4,5,6), and a high digit (7,8,9). Digits on a thermometer must increase from the bulb. A white circle joins consecutive digits, and a black circle joins digits with a 1:2 ratio. Cell shading is just for aesthetics.
1617: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage.
1618: Normal sudoku rules apply. The killer cage sums to 38; the marked diagonal sums to 15 and may include repeats. White dots join cells with consecutive digits; black dots join cells with a 1:2 ratio. Not all dots are given. Lines are palindromes, that read the same forward as backward. A digit shown in a larger circle must be in at least one of the four surrounding cells.
1619: Normal sudoku rules apply. A black dot joins cells with a ratio of 2:1; a white dot joins consecutive digits; an X joins cells that total ten and a V joins ones that total five - not all dots, Xs or Vs are shown. Digits may not repeat in killer cages but their sums will provide a message, from the simple mapping of 0-9==1-10 & A-Z==11-36 (e.g. a cage total of 30 would represent a "T" and 15 an "E").
1620: Normal sudoku rules apply. Apart from the central even cell, the grid must be filled with one or more pentominoes of each listed type, in which the top-left cell of the shape contains the given digit: 1=I, 2=W, 3=T, 4=L, 5=V, 6=X, 7=N, 8=Y, 9=P. Digits do not repeat in pentominoes, and two of the same type may not touch each other orthogonally. Cells joined by symbols are consecutive (white dot), have a ratio of 1:2 (black dot), or sum to five (V). Not all symbols are given.
1621: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on arrows sum to the total in the circle. Cells joined by a black dot have a ratio of 1:2; not all dots are shown. Row 5 text is just aesthetic.
1622: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat in rows, columns or regions. Digits in h, n & y shaped cages must sum to a total of either 20 or 22. Each colour/shape of cage has at least one instance of both alternative totals. A black dot between cells indicates that their values have a ratio of 2:1; & a white dot that their values are consecutive - not all dots are shown.
1623: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat in cages or on the ampersand (which therefore forms an additional region). All cages contain digits summing to the same total, which is to be determined. Letters represent the digits 1-9 in alphabetical order (so A=1, E=2, ..., R = 9). Cells separated by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Not all possible dots are given.
1624: Place 0-9 in each row, column and region. The four shaded 3x3 corner areas are magic squares. The four cages' totals must be determined and their product must be 500,000 (i.e. cageA*cageB*cageC*cageD=500,000). A 'V' between cells indicates that their values sum to five and an 'X' that their values sum to ten - not all Vs or Xs are shown.
1625: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits increase along the thermo from the bulb. Clues outside the grid show the sum of digits sandwiched between the 1 and the 9 in that row/column. The central 3x3 box is a magic square. 5s never have even neighbours, even considering the grid as a torus.
1626: Normal sudoku rules apply. An X joins two neighbouring cells that sum to 10, and a V joins two neighbouring cells that sum to 5. All Xs and Vs are given.
1627: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a thermo increase from the bulb. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the circle. Neighbouring digits on a green line must have a difference of at least 5.
1628: The players (open circles) will run their assigned routes and blocking schemes (arrows). To run the routes correctly, the digits along the arrows must sum to the number in the circle. The endzone (row 1) will be painted in alternating colors (of your choosing: the grey circles hold odd numbers; the grey squares hold even numbers.) There was a penalty flag thrown on the previous play (the X). It was a 10 yard penalty (meaning the 2 digits surrounding the X must sum to 10). Normal sudoku rules apply.
1629: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits joined by a white dot are consecutive. Digits joined by a black dot have a ratio of 1:2. Digits cannot repeat in each letter shape. Digits along a purple line are a consecutive set, not necessarily in order. Along the orange line, digits alternately increase or decrease.
1630: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Correctly entering digits will remove the fog in the surrounding cells. Each line has a distinct colour. Lines do not branch, cross, and only move orthoganally. All lines are renban (ie contain a set of non-repeating consecutive digits, in any order). All lines are “region sum” (ie along a line, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total (N). N may be different for each line.) All lines have a length of 3 or more. One line is also a thermometer and digits will increase from its bulb. (The bulb may be in the middle of the line.)
1631: Normal sudoku rules apply. White dots join cells with consecutive digits. Not all dots are given. The lowest common multiple of all digits on a connected grey line is lower than 10 (could be a different number for different lines).
1632: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by a black dot must contain digits in a ratio of 1:2 (ie one digit must be double the other). Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits. Not all possible dots are given. Cages are “Schrödinger cells” ie they contain one of 2 values. After filling all regular cells with digits, all Schrödinger cells must remain unresolved (in other words, both values of every Schrödinger cell must allow for a valid sudoku solution). The quantum balance of the universe is safe with this sudoku. Cats are safe too.
1633: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Each circle occupies a single cell (so no double-digit arrow totals are possible). In cages, digits sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. The grid is covered with fog. There are two initial light sources that illuminate the darkness and clear the fog. Put correct digits into the cells to get more light (it's ok to put a digit into a cell that is covered by fog). You have 5 lives to solve the puzzle. It costs 1 life for each wrong digit entered. Note: no guessing is required to finish the puzzle. The extra lives are given only to allow for possible typos.
1634: Normal sudoku rules apply: place digits 1-6 into every row, column and 3x2 box, once each. There are cars on the grid, and they carry given digits. The cars could be moved forward and backward in their direction, but they cannot drive through another car or through the grid border (they cannot escape from the grid). The given digits on the cars drive together with the car. Software tips: - Use the move button (4 arrows) for moving the cars. - You can hide the cars by pressing the yellow car button.
1635: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1636: Normal sudoku rules apply ie place digits 1-6 into each row, column and box without repeats. Most of the grid is covered in fog; placing correct digits (without guessing!) will clear the fog from adjacent cells. Digits in a cage cannot repeat and sum to the small clue in the top left corner (if given). Digits do not repeat on a blue line.
1637: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a blue line, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total. Different lines may have different totals. Each grey line consists of one or more contiguous groups of cells, each of which sums to 10. These groups of cells cannot overlap. Adjacent digits on a green line must differ by at least 5.
1638: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage may not repeat and sum to the number shown. Digits on a marked diagonal may not repeat.
1639: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cages sum to the total given. Clues outside the grid show the sum of the indicated diagonal, which can include repeat digits. Digits increase along thermos from the bulb. On the marked 9-cell diagonal, digits do not repeat. The green box is a magic square – each row, column and 3-cell diagonal sums to 15.
1640: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits increase from the bulb end. The white cells must be tiled with one copy each of the twelve possible pentominoes. If a pentomino contains a cell with a small number, its cells sum to that number. Digits in a pentomino may repeat if otherwise allowed.
1641: Normal sudoku rules apply. The white region is divided into 12 five-cell cages, one each of the 12 pentominoes. Digits may not repeat in a cage. A large moon indicates a boundary between cages whose totals differ by 1 if the moon is white and by a factor of 2 if the moon is black. A small moon indicates that two cells belong to the same cage: those cells differ by 1 if the moon is white and by a ratio of 2 if it is black. There may be undiscovered moons.
1642: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each purple line contains digits that sum to 15 (including the thermometer). Digits cannot repeat on a purple line. No two purple lines can contain the same set of digits. Digits along the purple thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Cells separated by a knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit.
1643: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cage totals are shown in the upper left corner of the cage. Inequalities between cells point to the small of the two digits. Nine cells in the grid are “multipliers”. If a multiplier appears in a cage, then it multiplies the sum of the other digits in the cage to produce the cage total. For instance, if a cage contains 3, 4, 5, 6 and 3 is the multiplier, the cage total would be 3*(4+5+6)=45. A multiplier which is not in a cage has no effect. Each row, each column, and each 3x3 box contains one multiplier, and each digit appears as a multiplier once.
1644: Each red cell either indexes the 5 in its row or in its column, i.e. it either equals the row of the 5 in its column, or the column of the 5 in its row. For instance, if r3c6 is a 7, then either r7c6 or r3c7 is a 5. Fives are antiknights: no two 5s can be a knight's move apart. Digits in a gray circle must be odd. A white dot joins a consecutive pair of digits.
1645: Place correct digits, shading, or loop lines into the cells to clear the fog. Contained within the grid are nine non-overlapping 3x3 square regions which must be located. Each region contains the digits 1 to 9 once each, and digits cannot repeat in any row or column. Cells outside regions do not contain digits and are considered "empty" for rules below. The digits in each cage sum to the clue in the top left corner, and may not repeat. Cages may include shaded and/or unshaded empty cells, but such cells do not contribute to the cage total. Shade some empty cells black so that no two shaded cells are orthogonally adjacent (including given shaded cells), and draw a non-intersecting loop through the centres of all unshaded empty cells. Arrow clues must contain a digit and be part of a 3x3 region; these clues represent the number of shaded cells in a straight line in the indicated direction. In the final grid, all cells will contain either a digit (with or without an arrow), a loop line, or black shading.
1646: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits joined by a white dot are consecutive, and digits joined by a black dot have a 1:2 ratio. Not all dots are given. A clue outside the grid either shows the sum of the digits between the 1 and the 9 in that row/column, INCLUDING 1 and 9, or the sum of the first X cells from that direction, where X is the first digit seen. The solver must determine which constraint applies to each clue.
1647: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along a green line must differ by at least 5. Each purple line contains a set of consecutive digits in any order. A clue outside the grid indicates the sum of the digits between the 1 and the 9 in the corresponding row or column.
1648: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a blue line must have an equal sum within each 3x3 box that line passes through, regardless of how many times the line exits and re-enters a region. The area outside the grid is considered one region for purposes of this rule. Different lines may have different sums. Numbers outside the grid give the sum of the first N digits in their respective row or column, where N is the digit nearest the clue (inside the grid). Eg The following statements describe how these lines must be interpreted (rows/columns 0 and 10 indicate cells outside the 9x9 grid): Box 1: r0c1 + r1c0 = r1c2 + r1c3 + r2c1 + r3c1 + r3c2 & Box 7: r8c0 + r10c3 = r7c1 + r8c1 + r9c1 + r9c2\n
1649: Normal sudoku rules apply. A digit X in a cage points to a second digit Y located X cells away vertically or horizontally. The number in the top left corner of the cage indicates the sum of X+Y. Digits in cages may point to cells inside or outside the grid. Clues outside the grid indicate the digit which has to be placed in the Nth cell in the corresponding direction, where N is the digit placed in the first cell in that direction. Digits along blue lines have the same sum within each region it passes through. The gray area outside the grid is considered one region for purposes of this rule. Different lines may have different sums.
1650: Normal Sudoku rules apply. In graves (cages), digits must sum to the day, month or year of the date on the grave. Digits cannot repeat within graves. Escape the graveyard by carefully plotting an orthogonally connected path between the green and red cells. The path may not cross the highest or lowest digits in a grave.
1651: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Along green lines, adjacent digits must have a difference of at least 5. Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits. Cells separated by a black dot must contain digits with a ratio of 1:2. Not all dots are given.
1652: Normal sudoku rules apply. In graves (cages), digits must sum to the day, month or year of the date on the grave. Digits cannot repeat within graves. Escape the graveyard by carefully plotting an orthogonally connected path between the green and red cells. The path may not cross the highest or lowest digits in a grave.
1653: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Navigate the maze by carefully plotting an orthogonally connected path from the green cell to the red cell. The path must include every cell containing an arrow, first entering the bulb and then travelling directly along the arrow. Every cell in the grid is associated with a cardinal direction (NESW), given by its digit modulo 4. The path must exit every cell it enters according to these directions. Which direction corresponds to which digits is to be discovered.
1654: Detective, after bad weather we have finally been able reach the island following the distress call. Though we are yet to identify each victim, it appears that all ten digits died in accordance with the following verse: Ten little digits sat down to dine; One was evenly spread in a sandwich and then there were nine. Nine little digits under white cliffs slept late; One was crushed by stones and then there were eight. Eight little digits heard whispers of heaven; One collapsed in the crossing and then there were seven. Seven little digits cut up renban sticks; One chopped itself symmetrically and then there were six. Six little digits played with bows and knives; An arrow tip pierced one and then there were five. Five little digits were tried under law; One was shot for different parity and then there were four. Four little digits took a trip out to sea; A red herring swallowed one and then there were three. Three little digits got stuck together with glue; One was squashed between the others and then there were two. Two little digits lay under the sun; One melted at peak temperature and then there was one. One little digit with nowhere to run; Oddly still killed and then there were none. We have also found a note, where one unidentified digit confesses to the murder of the other nine. We believe you should be able to solve the mystery by filling in the grid legitimately with the nine victims, leaving out the murderer. A few extra details from the note: Normal sudoku variant rules apply. Sandwich crusts have been marked with thin rectangles and contain the highest and lowest digits in the grid. Each line of the rhyme refers only to the remaining digits. Some victims have been identified by cages in the grid.
1655: Normal sudoku rules almost apply. Place the digits 0-9 into cells such that each digit appears once in every row, column and region. To accommodate this, one cell in each row, column and region is a Schrödinger cell, which contains two digits. In graves (cages), digits must sum to the day, month or year of the date on the grave. Digits cannot repeat within graves. Escape the graveyard by carefully plotting an orthogonally connected path between the green and red cells. The path may not cross the highest or lowest digits in a grave.
1656: It’s the first advent Sunday and we want to go for a walk. Nala doesn’t know where we planned to go yet so it’s a surprise for her and she loves to explore her surroundings! Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Help Nala find the path around the lake by following these rules: The path must be orthogonally connected and visit all cells of all cages. The path forms a loop (ie it has no start or end points). The path can touch itself diagonally, however it is not allowed to touch orthogonally (ie no cell on the path can share edges with more than two other cells on the path). Digits along the path differ by AT MOST 2. Cells separated by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Cells separated by a black dot contain digits in a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit is double the other). Not all possible dots are given. The grid is partially covered in fog. Placing correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells, possibly revealing more clues.
1657: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along arrows must sum to the digit in the attached circle. Digits may repeat on arrows if allowed by other rules. Arrows do not cross or overlap in any way. Placing correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells, possibly revealing more clues.
1658: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw 3 snakes which must each begin and end at a different grey spot. Snakes are lines which may move orthogonally and diagonally between cells. They may touch each other (or themselves), and can even cross each other, but they must not branch, share cells with each other, or enter cages. A digit on a snake indicates exactly how many times that digit appears on that snake. Eg: If there is a 5 on a snake, there are five 5s on that snake. One snake is a “German Whisper” line; along it, adjacent digits must differ by at least 5. One snake is a “slow thermometer”; along this line, reading from one end to the other, digits must always increase or stay the same. One snake is “entropic”; along it, any group of 3 adjacent cells must contain one low digit (1, 2 or 3), one medium digit (4, 5 or 6) and one high digit (7, 8 or 9.) Digits in a cage must sum to the small clue given in that cage. Digits separated by a V sum to 5.
1659: Normal sudoku rules apply. The digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in the circled cell. Digits must not repeat at corresponding box positions.
1660: Normal sudoku rules apply. Any set of three sequential cells along a teal modular line contains one digit from (1,4,7), one digit from (2,5,8), and one digit from (3,6,9). Digits an equal distance from the centre of a lavender 'Zipper Line' sum to the digit in the middle of that line.
1661: Normal sudoku rules apply. A 2-digit ‘Taco clue’ XY outside the grid gives the sum of X + Y + the digits between X and Y in the indicated row or column. Example: A valid taco sum for 18 could be 8361.
1662: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits joined by a white dot are consecutive. Digits joined by a black dot are in a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit must be double the other). Not all dots are given. For each line, one attached circle contains an odd digit and the other circle contains an even digit. The odd digit indicates the number of odd digits along the line (not including itself), and the even digit indicates the number of even digits along the line (not including itself). Shade some cells such that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected and all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected. No 2x2 area may be fully shaded or fully unshaded. The circles also act as "minesweeper" clues. Cells containing a circle are always unshaded, and their value is the number of shaded cells in the surrounding 3x3 area (i.e. the up to eight cells that touch the circle either orthogonally or diagonally).
1663: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Placing correct digits reveals clues in the surrounding area. If the grid is rotated 180 degrees, the matching cells add up to 10 e.g. R3C2+R7C8=10. For this purpose, the puzzle's central digit adds to itself. Digits an equal distance from the center of a lavender 'Zipper Line' sum to the digit in the middle of that line. Adjacent digits on a green line differ by 5 or more. All lines are exactly 5 cells long, only move orthogonally and don't share cells with other lines.
1664: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a lavender zipper line, any pair of digits that are the same distance from the centre cell of the line (marked by a spot) sum to the digit in that centre cell.
1665: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage don't repeat and sum to the given clue in the top left corner of the cage (the clue is always given and must be located in the leftmost cell of the uppermost row of the cage.) Digits separated by a white dot are consecutive digits. Additionally the grid is partially covered in fog. Placing correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells, possibly revealing more clues.
1666: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a blue line, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total. Blue lines may have different totals to one another. The digit in the grey square is even. Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits.
1667: Normal sudoku rules apply. One cell in every row, column and box is a doubler. This cell counts as double its value on the lines. Each of the digits 1 to 9 appears exactly once in a doubler cell. One cell in every row, column and box is a tripler. This cell counts as triple its value on the lines. Each of the digits 1 to 9 appears exactly once in a tripler cell. Doublers and triplers do not share cells and no doubler or tripler cell is within a king's move of any other doubler or tripler cell. Lines are Region Sum Lines: the values of the digits on each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total (say a total of X). If a line passes through a box more than once, each line segment in that box must sum to X separately. Each blue lines may have a different value for X.
1668: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits an equal distance from the centre of a lavender 'Zipper Line' must sum to the digit in the middle of that line.
1669: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each blue line is an equal sum line. All digits along a blue line must sum to the same total in each 3x3 box the line visits. Different blue lines may have different total sums. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in the circle of that arrow. Cells separated by a black dot are in the ratio 1 to 2. Cells separated by a white dot are consecutive. Not all possible dots are given.
1670: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw a snake which starts at a grey circle and ends at the other grey circle, and never passes through a grey square. The snake moves orthogonally and/or diagonally and can cross itself and acts as a slow thermometer i.e. reading from one end to the other, digits on the snake increase or stay the same (the direction must be determined by the solver). Furthermore, the snake passes through at least 27 cells. The sum of the digits within a cage must sum to the small clue in the top-left corner of that cage.
1671: Normal sudoku rules apply. Connect each pair of matching coloured spots with a snake. Snakes may only move orthogonally through the grid, not diagonally. They may touch each other (and themselves) but cannot share cells. Each pair of adjacent digits along a snake has the same difference, but this 'difference value' may be different for different snakes. A grey square contains an even digit. A black dot connects two digits with a 1:2 ratio (one is double the other.)
1672: Normal sudoku rules apply. If the digits at each end of a line are X and Y, then the first X digits on the line starting from X must sum to the same total as the first Y digits on the line starting from Y. (X and Y need not necessarily be different numbers; X and Y may not exceed the number of cells on the line).
1673: Santa needs your help to deliver his gifts in the snowstorm!! Place the digits from 1-6 twice in every row, column and region. Normal Japanese sums rules apply. Colors used in this puzzle are beige, brown, dark brown, red and grey/black. The squares outside the grid indicate the order of runs of contiguous cells found in that row or column that must be shaded the color of the clue. The number in the clue, if given, indicates the sum of the cells in the run. There must be at least one unshaded cell between runs of the same color, though there is no need between runs of differing colors. All runs are given. White snow dots separate consecutive digits.
1674: [GATHER SNOW] Winter Sudoku Rules apply: Place the digits 0-8 in every row, column, and 3x3 box. [HEAD & BODY] Digits along arrows sum to the digit in the corresponding circle. [EYES] Digits joined by a white dot are consecutive [NOSE] Digits along the orange thermometer increase from the bulb end. [BUTTONS] Digits joined by a black dot are in a ratio of 2:1. [ARMS] Adjacent digits along green lines must have a difference of 5 or greater. [MAKE IT UNIQUE] Digits joined by a blue snowflake form a unique domino—those digits cannot appear next to each other orthogonally anywhere else in the grid.
1675: Gather around the tree! Divide the green area into pentominoes, i.e. orthogonally-connected groups of 5 cells. No two pentominoes have the same shape even when rotated or reflected. Digits may not repeat in a pentomino. The tree has ornaments (dots) of several colours. If a pentomino contains a green dot, it is a Germanimo: adjacent pairs of digits inside it differ by at least 5. If it contains a red dot, it is a Renbanimo: it contains 5 consecutive digits. Black, white, and silver dots show a boundary between two pentominoes. Black means their totals are in a 1:2 ratio. White means their totals differ by one. Silver means their totals are equal. Along a thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end.
1676: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a line, the sum of digits on the line is the same in each region the line passes through. The sum may be different for different lines.
1677: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on a grey line must sum to 7, 8 or 9.
1678: Place the digits 0-9, once each, into every row, column and 3x3 box. To enable this, one cell in every row, column and 3x3 box is a “Schrödinger cell” that contains two digits. This cell counts as the sum of its digits for the purposes of the zipper line rule below. Digits an equal distance from the circled centre of a lavender zipper line sum to the same number. The grid is partially covered in fog. Placing correct digits reveals clues in the surrounding 3x3 area. For the avoidance of doubt, if two strands of the same zipper line enter a single cell then the digit in that cell must be counted twice in determining its contribution to the line.
1679: Normal sudoku rules apply. Reading from the bulb end to the tip, digits along a thermometer must either increase or stay the same.
1680: Normal sudoku rules apply. Choose a number out of the four numbers 7, 8, 12, and 13. The sum of the digits in each cage is the number you have chosen. Along a thermometer, digits increase from the bulb to the tip. A white dot connects consecutive digits.
1681: 1-8 must be placed, once each, in every row, column and marked region. A purple line contains a sequence of consecutive digits in any order. Cells separated by an X sum to 10. Cells separated by a V sum to 5. All possible Xs and Vs are given.
1682: Place 1-7 in each row, column and marked region. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in the attached circle. Digits may repeat on an arrow if allowed by other rules.
1683: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers outside the grid are little killer clues, look-and-say little killer clues and sandwich clues: Digits along diagonals indicated by arrows sum to the number given. Also, the first digit in a clue indicates the number of times the second digit in the clue appears along the indicated diagonal. Also, a clue outside the grid shows the sum of the digits sandwiched between the 1 and the 9 in that row/column. Cells separated by an V sum to 5.
1684: Divide the grid into eight 2x4 boxes. Each box could be placed either horizontally or vertically. Fill the grid with the digits 1-8, so that no digit repeats in a row, column or box. A digit in a circle indicates exactly how many circles contain that digit. Digits joined by a small white dot are consecutive. Not all possible white dots are shown.
1685: Place the digits 0-9 once each into every row, column and 2x2 box. Cells may contain up to four digits simultaneously, and cells in the same row/column/box may not contain the same number of digits. A cell's value is the sum of the digits it contains. Values separated by a white dot are consecutive. Values separated by a black dot are in a 1:2 ratio. Values separated by an X sum to 10.
1686: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a thick magenta line form a consecutive sequence without repeats, in any order. Digits connected by a thin green line must differ by at least 5.
1687: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on the marked diagonal must not repeat. Digits separated by a king’s move must not repeat. The grid contains a number of bidirectional thermometers (ie: digits must increase from the bulb end, but the bulb end is not known). Each thermometer contains either all odd or all even digits. The blue and red thermometers are special: Firstly, the position of their bulbs are known and are coloured. Secondly, the blue bulb is colder than the red bulb (ie: it contains a lower digit). Thirdly, the blue thermometer is colder than the red thermometer (ie: the sum of its digits is lower).
1688: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits on arrows must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Digits on grey palindrome lines must read the same in both directions. (Arrows are different colours purely to clarify which arrow is which when they cross.)
1689: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages must sum to the cage total. The digit on the circle is odd. Digits on a purple line form a consecutive set in any order. Digits on purple lines can also be used to index the cell's column number in its row. For example, if R3C1 was a 7, then 1 would have to be positioned in R3C7.
1690: Each row, column, and nine cell region must contain the digits 1 to 9, once each. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1691: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered by fog and correctly placing digits may reveal additional digits. Each digit satisfies only one of the following conditions: a) It is exactly one chess knight's move away from at least one cell containing the same digit; b) It is in its own 3x3 box (3x3 boxes are arranged in normal reading order. So eg 9 in box 9 meets this condition). c) It is the digit 5. There is one exception: the digit in the very centre of the grid satisfies exactly two conditions. No guessing is required or allowed.
1692: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits must not repeat on the marked diagonal. Digits in cages must sum to the cage total. Each N-sum line can be divided into two or more non-overlapping groups of adjacent digits that sum to N. No two lines have the same value for N.
1693: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages cannot repeat and must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits an equal distance from the centre of a blue zipper line must sum to the same total. For odd length lines, the total is the digit in the centre of the line. The grey line is a palindrome and must read the same forwards and backwards. A digit on any line also indicates how many times that digit appears on all lines in the puzzle.
1694: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a line must be between the digits in the connected circles ie greater than the lower of the two circled digits and lower than the greater of the two circled digits. The digits on the lines must allow the smallest possible difference between the numbers on their circles. A difference of zero is possible.
1695: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in the connected circle. Digits may repeat along arrows if allowed by other rules. The four caged regions are clones of each other, with rotation allowed but not required. This means that the same digit must appear in the center of each clone, and the outer 4 digits must form the same sequence of digits when read clockwise from any particular digit.
1696: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in the connected circle. Digits may repeat along an arrow if allowed by the other rules.
1697: Divide the grid into 9 regions, each containing 9 orthogonally connected cells. Fill every row, column, and region with the digits 1-9 once each. A few region border segments are already given. Blue lines are "region sum lines". ie For a given line, the region borders separate the line into two or more segments with equal sums. Distinct segments within the same region are not summed together.
1698: Fill each box with the digits 1-9 once each. Digits may not repeat in any row, column, or same relative box position (e.g. the bottom left corner of each box). Digits in cages sum to the number given. Adjacent digits on green lines differ by at least 5. Adjacent digits on purple lines are consecutive.
1699: Normal sudoku rules apply. Minimal between lines: Digits on a line must be between the digits in the connected circles. The difference between the circled digits must be as small as allowed by normal sudoku rules. For example, a circle in R1C2 connected with a straight line to a circle in R5C6 would have a difference of 2 because it is possible (and necessary) to repeat the same digit in all 3 spots along the line. Clones: The grey 4x4 regions must contain the same digits in the same arrangement. Skyscrapers: Each digit N in the grid represents a building of height N. Numbers outside the grid indicate how many buildings can be seen from that direction in the row, with taller buildings blocking shorter buildings from being seen.
1700: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle/pill. The two digit pill total is read from top down. Digits in cells separated by X must sum to 10. Not all Xs are given.
1701: Normal sudoku rules apply. Identical digits cannot be a knight’s move apart. Along thermos, digits increase from the bulb. Cages show their sums. In the original puzzle, three given digits are shown as pencil-marks. After the puzzle is finished, erase all the digits apart from 1s, slide the 1s 3 cells to the right, or 6 cells to the left, and re-solve the puzzle ignoring the pencil-marks!
1702: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage (if given). Digits cannot repeat within a cage.
1703: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers outside the grid show the total of the X number of cells, starting the OPPOSITE side of the grid, where X is the first cell next to the clue, so if r1 began with a 4, its last 4 cells would sum to 22.
1704: Normal sudoku rules apply. A clue outside the grid shows the total of the X number of cells, starting on the OPPOSITE side of the grid, where X is the first cell next to the clue. Cages show their totals.
1705: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. The purple line contains a set of consecutive digits. Digits may not repeat along the marked diagonal.
1706: Normal sudoku rules apply. The middle dot is the centre of the “galaxy”. The galaxy is 180° rotationally symmetric and orthogonally connected. Digits in cages that are not part of the galaxy sum to the given total (in the cage’s top left corner).
1707: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Placing a correct digit will clear the fog from the surrounding cells. Values of the pair of cells with an equal distance to the circled centre of a lavender line sum to the value in that central cell. Shade some cells orange such that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected and all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected. No 2x2 area may be fully shaded or fully unshaded. The value of a shaded cell is its digit. The value of an unshaded cell is zero minus its digit (a negative number).
1708: Normal sudoku rules apply. Additionally, no digit may appear more than once on a particular clue type. Type 1: Digits on a purple line form a set of non-repeating, consecutive digits in any order. Type 2: Along green lines, adjacent digits must differ by at least 5. Type 3: Digits separated by a black dot have a 1:2 ratio, meaning one is exactly double the other. Type 4: Digits along a grey thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Type 5: Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1709: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid contains nine "Doubler Fruit", one in each row, column, and box. Each tree has exactly one doubler fruit, which is on one branch tip. Five other fruit are scattered around the orchard. Cells containing a doubler fruit count as double their digit value. Each digit from 1 through 9 is doubled exactly once. Along the grey "Thermo Tree" values must increase from the bulb end. Along the pink "Renban Tree" values form a non-repeating consecutive sequence. Along a blue "Region Sum Tree" values have an equal sum N within each box it passes through. Where the line passes through the same box more than once, each individual segment sums to N separately. Different lines may have different values for N. Values in cages sum to the given clue.
1710: Normal sudoku rules apply. A digit in a circled cell indicates the total number of times that digit appears in circled cells in the grid. Lines connecting circled cells are “Between Lines”. Digits on a “Between Line” must have values between those of the digits on that line's circled endpoints.
1711: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers outside the grid (including those on lines extending outside the grid) are X-Sums, which sum the first X digits from the clue, where X is the first digit seen. Along the grey thermos, values must increase from the bulb end. Along the pink renban lines, values must form a non-repeating consecutive sequence in any order. Along the blue region sum lines values have an equal sum N within each box they pass through. Different lines may have different values of N. Values in cages sum to the given clue.
1712: Mean mini sudoku: place six distinct NUMBERS from 1-9 in each row, column and box without repeats. Lines with circled cells and mathematical operators between them must contain a true mathematical equation. Oh, yeah, you probably already guessed it, but the numbers don't have to be integers. They must be real, though.
1713: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Diagonals must contain the digits 1-9 exactly once. The inequality sign points to the lower of the two cells it connects. The black dot indicates that one of the connected cells must be double the other. The "taxicab" distance between two cells is the minimum number of orthogonal moves required to go from cell A to cell B. In the completed grid, ONLY the red cells contain digits that are their taxicab distance away from another cell containing the same digit. For example, if cell A and B both contain 8 and had a taxicab distance of 8 between them then they MUST both be red. No two white cells have this property. Of the set of digits 1 to 9, only a subset (whose sum is less than 15) can appear in the red squares.
1714: Normal sudoku rules apply. In addition, both marked diagonals contain the digits 1-9 exactly once. If two consecutive digits are adjacent in the completed grid, the edge between them is marked with a white dot. Similarly, if two digits along the two main diagonals are consecutive, they have been separated by a grey dot. All possible white and grey dots are provided. If two cells contain the same digit, the "taxicab distance" cannot be equal to that digit. The "taxicab distance" is the minimum number of orthogonal moves from cell A to cell B. For example, if there is a 4 in R3C4, there cannot be a 4 in R2C7, since it takes a minimum of 4 moves to go from R3C4 to R2C7.
1715: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Place some blocks in the grid. Digits in grey cells will be the clues for the number of blocks in the given direction. Blocks cannot touch orthogonally. The remainder of the grid (not blocks or clues) must be a part of a single continuous non-intersecting loop. Also, the loop can only turn in a cell containing an odd digit.
1716: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells with arrows are the Yajisan-Kazusan clues except that the valid clues give the sum of all the shaded cells in that direction (ie NOT the number of shaded cells). All other basic Y-K rules apply.
1717: Normal sudoku rules apply, and digits in cages sum to 10 including no repeated digits. No other potential 10-cages can be created in the grid, although each of the given cages has at least one potential killer cage of size 10 overlapping it.
1718: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along the blue lines increase and decrease alternately.
1719: Normal sudoku rules apply. Lines act both as Arrows, so that numbers on a line, including the blue circle, sum to the number in the orange circle, and as Between Lines, so any number on a line is between the numbers in the connected circles.
1720: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along the marked diagonal must not repeat. Digits along grey lines increase starting from the bulb end. Coloured lines are palindromes, reading the same forwards or backwards. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the circled cell.
1721: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a thermometer must increase from the bulb end.
1722: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on the E and R must differ by at least 5. Digits on a light grey thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Digits on a purple line must be a set of consecutive digits in any order, and must not repeat. Digits in a cage do not repeat, and must sum to the total given. Digits on a marked diagonal must sum to the total given. Digits separated by a white dot are consecutive.
1723: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on an arrow sum to the value in the attached circle. Digits in a cage may not repeat and sum to the total given. Purple dots are pivot points for constraint clues, which rotate clockwise around their pivot point through N steps of 90 degrees, where N is the value on the pivot. Rotated clues may overlap but must not extend outside the grid.
1724: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by a single knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Digits may repeat along an arrow if allowed by other rules. In cages, digits sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Cells sharing a black dot have a 1:2 ratio (and not all possible dots are given). Clues outside the grid give the sum of the digits along the indicated diagonal. The digits on a diagonal may repeat.
1725: Normal sudoku rules apply: Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Cells containing a grey square contain an even digit; those with a grey circle contain an odd digit. The clue outside the grid gives the sum of the indicated diagonal, which may include repeats. White dots separate cells containing consecutive digits. Not all white dots are given.
1726: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1727: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each purple line contains a consecutive set of non-repeating digits in any order. Cells separated by a black dot contain digits with a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit must be double the other). Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits. Not all dots are given.
1728: Normal sudoku rules apply. Circled digits must be the mean (average) of any arrows that leave the circle. Cells separated by a black dot contain digits with a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit is double the other). Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits. Not all possible dots are given.
1729: Normal sudoku rules apply. Golden lines form sets of non-repeating digits where no digits can be consecutive. Cells with grey circles contain odd digits; cells with grey squares contain even digits.
1730: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat on the indicated diagonal. Cages show their sums. Digits in cells separated by a white dot are consecutive. Digits in cells separated by a black dot have a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit is double the other).
1731: Normal sudoku rules apply. The digits outside the grid must appear in one of the first three cells of the row or column as seen from that direction. Digits in a cage must sum to the number in the top left corner of the cage. Digits may not repeat within a cage.
1732: Normal sudoku rules apply. There are 18 cages in the grid. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Each cage has exactly one partner such that, when combined together, they would form a valid 9-cell cage (ie containing no repeated digits). Along a thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end. Cells with grey squares must contain even digits.
1733: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers increase from the bulb to the end of the thermometers. Digits along the blue line must sum to the same number in each 3x3 box the line visits, for each visit. Adjacent digits along the green line have a difference of at least five. Cells separated by an X sum to 10. Not all Xs are given.
1734: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. For the avoidance of doubt, all arrows in this puzzle are straight lines.
1735: Normal sudoku rules apply. On a green line adjacent digits must have a difference of at least 5. Digits on an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1736: Place the digits 0–8 once each in every row, column, and 3x3 box. A digit in a circle must appear at least once in the four surrounding cells. That digit also equals the number of surrounding cells that are shaded. A “?” represents the same number for both clues within a circle (i.e. that digit appears and that many cells are shaded). The value of “?” may differ between circles. Unshaded cells in the grid must be orthogonally connected, and unshaded cells that are orthogonally adjacent must have digits that differ by at least 5.
1737: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by an X contain digits summing to 10. 'Beachcomber' rules apply ie A digit N in a circle means that a total of N digits smaller than N are visible in all orthogonal directions from the circle (ie looking North, South, East & West). Digits larger than N block the view.
1738: Digits do not repeat in any row, column, marked region or or marked diagonal. Each orange line in the grid serves three purposes: it is a palindrome (digits on it must read the same in both directions, e.g 94349); it is also a thermometer (pair) with its bulb in the centre of the line; and it is also a pair of arrows that meet in the centre with circles at the ends. The shared arrow digit is in the thermometer bulb and digits on thermometers must strictly increase from the bulb. A white dot between cells indicates that their digits are consecutive - not all dots are shown.
1739: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat within a cage. Cage clues show the sum of the digits in the cage plus the sum of all digits that aren't in any cage. For example, if the digits 1, 2, and 3 are always placed outside of cages, and all other digits appear in a cage at least once, then all cages have 6 (=1+2+3) added to their total. A "Greater Than" sign between two cells points to the smaller digit.
1740: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into 4 sections of orthogonally-connected cells such that each section shares an edge with every other section and no 2x2 area is occupied by only one section. Cells on the same line belong to the same section. Each section has a different constraint, which ALL of its lines must obey. The constraints for each section are: i) RENBAN: Digits on a line do not repeat and form a consecutive set, in any order; ii) PALINDROME: The digits along a line read the same forwards and backwards; iii) GERMAN WHISPER: Adjacent digits on a line must have a difference of at least 5; iv) REGION SUM: Along a line, if it crosses a 3x3 box border, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total. The sum may be different for different lines.
1741: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by an X contain digits summing to 10. Multiplying the digits on each end of a brown line gives the sum of all digits on that line. For example, a line could have the digits 3-5-4, because 3x4 = 3+5+4.
1742: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw 12 orthogonally connected regions of different sizes which do not overlap. The regions do not need to cover the entire grid. Within a region, a digit may only repeat if it appears on a gold ring, in which case it can only appear on gold rings. A digit on a gold ring indicates the number of gold rings within its region. A digit on a pear tree is equal to the number of cells in its region. The 3 digits on red baubles sum to 25.
1743: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into rectangular regions which do not overlap. Each region must include exactly two circled cells, and the digits in those cells indicate the width and height of that region (in either order). Digits on a line must have a value between the digits in the two attached circles.
1744: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits which are an equal distance from the center of a lavender 'zipper' line have the same sum. For odd length lines, that sum is also the central digit.
1745: Normal sudoku rules apply. Neighbouring digits along a green line must differ by at least 5. White dots connect consecutive digits; black dots connect digits with a 2:1 ratio. Not all dots are given.
1746: Place the digits 1 to 9 once each into every row, column and 3x3 box. Shade some cells in the grid such that all shaded cells are connected orthogonally and all unshaded cells are connected orthogonally. No 2x2 box may be fully shaded or fully unshaded. Clues outside the grid give the sum of the first continuous block of shaded cells seen from that direction. Blue cages are "vaults". Digits MAY repeat within a vault. Any digit within a vault must not appear in any cells orthogonally adjacent to that vault. The largest digit in any given vault is equal to the number of shaded cells inside that vault.
1747: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells such that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected and all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected and no 2x2 area may be fully shaded or unshaded. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. The digit in the arrow circle is equal to the sum of all shaded cells in the direction of the arrow tip (beginning from the next cell after the arrow tip).
1748: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells in the grid such that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected and all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected; and no 2x2 area is fully shaded or fully unshaded. Candles illuminate the grid and must be unshaded. A digit on a candle is equal to the number of consecutive unshaded cells (including itself) the candle sees in its row and column
1749: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each cell in the grid has to be marked either hot or cold such that i) all hot cells form a single orthononally connected region; ii) all cold cells form a single orthogonally connected region; and iii) no 2x2 area is entirely hot or cold. Values on a thermometer must be increasing from the bulb to the tip. Cold cells on a thermometer are considered to be negative values.
1750: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on a green line differ by at least 5. Cages must contain an equal number of low (1,2,3,4) and high (6,7,8,9) digits AND an equal number of even (2,4,6,8) and odd (1,3,7,9) digits. Digits CAN repeat in cages, but they cannot contain 5.
1751: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits increase from the bulb.
1752: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits increase from the bulb.
1753: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the 'pill', reading left-to-right - all numbers in pills are unique 2-digit numbers. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end.
1754: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the attached circle.
1755: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the circle.
1756: Normal sudoku rules apply. A grey line is a palindrome, reading the same backwards and forwards.
1757: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. In this puzzle, all circles must contain different digits.
1758: Normal Sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. An odd snake has made the grid its home! You must deduce the cells where the snake begins and ends. The snake has the following properties: the snake's body consists solely of odd digit cells; the snake visits all 9 boxes; the snake does not touch itself orthogonally (Diagonals are fine); the snake does not orthogonally touch any odd digit cell that is not part of its body (Diagonals are fine).
1759: Normal sudoku rules apply. Black dots join cells with a 1:2 ratio; white dots join cells with consecutive digits. A 1/2 pair can be joined by a black or white dot. Not all dots are given.
1760: Normal sudoku rules apply. A pentomino is a set of 5 orthogonally connected cells. There are exactly 12 different possible pentomino shapes (treating reflections/rotations as equivalent). Arrange all 12 pentominoes in the grid so that 9 of them contain only odd digits. Digits CAN repeat inside a pentomino. Pairs of cells connected by an X or V sum to 10 or 5 respectively AND belong to two separate pentominoes. Not every X and V is given. Along the thermometer, digits increase from the bulb end.
1761: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a circle must appear at least once in the four cells touching the circle. Around each circle, at most one cell can contain an odd digit. All cells containing odd digits form a single orthogonally-connected region.
1762: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must sum to the given total. Except... One of the digits, 1-9, is poison. If a cage contains the poisoned digit, then digits in the cage must NOT sum to the given total. Digits in a cage may not repeat, regardless of poison.
1763: Normal sudoku rules apply. In each cage, digits do not repeat and sum to the given total. A digit in a circle indicates how many times that digit appears in circles.
1764: Normal sudoku rules apply. Clues outside the grid show the sums of the odd digits between the 2 and the 8 in that row/column.
1765: Normal Sudoku rules apply. In addition no L-shaped tetromino can contain four consecutive digits (for instance you can't have r2c9=5,r4c9=8). The little killer clue indicates cells on the indicated diagonal must sum to 40 and may contain repeated digits.
1766: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Each sandwich clue indicates either the sum of odd digits between the 2 and 8 or the sum of even digits between the 1 and 9 in that row/column.
1767: Normal Sudoku rules apply. In each column, any cage of N≥2 cells must contain a run of N consecutive digits sorted in descending order, starting from the top. Negative constraints apply, e.g. 8 cannot be immediately above 7 unless both cells are in the same cage.
1768: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits do not repeat in cages, and multiply together to give the number shown in the cage. The grey circle represents an odd digit.
1769: Normal killer Sudoku (so, as usual, numbers cannot repeat in a cage). In addition, numbers outside the grid indicate the sum of cells "sandwiched" between the 1 and the 9 in the relevant column/row.
1770: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end.
1771: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits between 1 and 9 sum to the clue outside the grid.
1772: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the number given in top corner and do not repeat.
1773: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers outside the grid give the first hidden skyscraper from that direction.
1774: Normal sudoku rules apply. In cages, digits must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits cannot repeat within a cage.
1775: Normal sudoku rules apply. Orthogonally adjacent digits may not be consecutive. Adjacent digits along a green line must differ by at least 5. A clue outside the grid gives the sum of the indicated diagonal.
1776: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw a snake that starts and ends at a purple spot and has a purple spot exactly at its centre. The snake can only move orthogonally from cell to cell, and may not touch itself, not even diagonally. The snake functions as a “zipper line” ie any pair of digits that are an equal distance from the central spot sum to the digit on that central spot. Any pair of cells connected by a clue (dot, diamond, X or V) must either both be on the snake, or both be off the snake. Cells connected by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Cells connected by black dot contain digits in a 1:2 ratio (ie one is double the other.) Cells connected by a green dot must contain digits with a difference of at least 5. Cells connected by a red diamond contain digits with the same parity (ie both are odd or both are even.) Cells connected by an X contain digits summing to 10. Cells connected by a V contain digits summing to 5.
1777: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Placing correct digits reveals clues in the surrounding 3x3 area. Digits separated by a brown dot are either consecutive or in a 1:2 ratio. Not all dots are necessarily given.
1778: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a purple Renban Line are a set of consecutive digits in some order. Every set of three adjacent digits along a peach Entropic Line contains one low digit (123), one middle digit (456), and one high digit (789).
1779: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages sum to the small clue in the top left corner. Digits do not repeat in cages. Digits separated by a white dot differ by one (not all such dots are shown).
1780: Normal sudoku rules apply. The 3x3 grey squares are additional regions of the puzzle whereby digits cannot repeat within a grey square. The YNWA lines (in boxes 2,4,6, and 8) are GERMAN whisper lines ie adjacent digits upon the line must differ by at least 5. A digit in a football (white circle) indicates how many footballs contain that digit.
1781: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Cells separated by a single knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit.
1782: Normal sudoku rules apply. A digit in column 1 indicates the column in which the digit 1 appears in that row. (Eg If r4c1 is a 6, r4c6 is a 1). A digit in column 5 indicates the column in which the digit 5 appears in that row. A digits in column 9 indicates the column in which the digit 9 appears in that row. Digits in cells with a shaded square must be even. Cells separated by a single knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit.
1783: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage cannot repeat and must sum to the small clue in top left corner of the cage. However nine cells in the grid are “doublers”. A digit in such a cell counts as double its value towards the cage sums. There is exactly one doubler in each row, column, and 3x3 box – and the doublers form a set of the digits 1 to 9.
1784: Place a digit in each cell such that in any row, column, or 3x3 box, if a digit is present, it appears exactly its own number of times (in that row, column, 3x3 box). Digits may not repeat within a cage.
1785: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, values strictly increase from the bulb end. There are nine doubler cells in the grid, one in every row, column and box. Each digit from 1-9 appears in a doubler cell exactly once. A doubler cell's value counts as double its digit.
1786: Divide the grid along the grid lines into regions called polyominoes. Place a number inside each cell equal to the total area (in number of cells) of the polyomino it belongs to. No two polyominoes with the same area, or with areas that differ by one, can share an edge. The number at the top left of each cage gives the sum of all numbers that appear inside of it. Numbers may be repeated in cages. [Answer check will work if cells are filled with just the units digit of their numbers.]
1787: Normal sudoku rules apply. Every adjacent pair of digits along the contains no repeats and sums to 13 or 14. Digits in cages do not repeat and must sum to 13 or 14. Digits along the arrow (which may repeat) sum to the value in the attached circle.
1788: Normal sudoku rules apply. Values an equal distance to the circled centre of a lavender “zipper” line sum to the value of the central digit. Nine cells (one in each row, column and 3x3 box) contain a “Mirrored Digit”. A Mirrored Digit takes the value opposite to its digit on the 1-9 scale. (In other words, 1 takes the value of 9, 2 the value of 8... 9 the value of 1.) Each digit 1-9 is mirrored once. Unmirrored digits use their digits as values.
1789: Normal sudoku rules apply. Box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum.
1790: Normal sudoku rules apply. There is an orange snake in the grid, which moves from one cell center to the next horizontally or vertically (i.e., never diagonally). It may not touch itself orthogonally. The snake divides the non-snake cells into 8 different regions, one of each size from 1-8 cells. Each of these regions is orthogonally contiguous and acts like a killer cage. Each cage encloses exactly one sum clue, which indicates the sum of the digits in that cage, and digits may not repeat in any cage. (The sum clue need not be in the top left corner of the cage). The snake itself is a so-called 'Dutch Whisper' line, i.e. neighboring digits on the snake must differ by 4 or more. The white dot joins consecutive digits.
1791: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Digits cannot repeat along a blue main diagonal.
1792: Normal sudoku rules apply. Binairo rules apply: A run of 3 even digits never occurs in a row or column and, a run of 3 odd digits never occurs in a row or column. Each even/odd pattern must be different in the rows, and each even/odd pattern must be different in the columns. Digits increase along the thermo from the bulb. Digits separated by an X add to 10, digits separated by a V add to 5.
1793: Normal sudoku rules apply. Blue lines are ‘region sum lines’ ie 3x3 box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum. Brown lines are ‘product sum lines’ ie the digits on each end of the line must multiply together to give the sum of ALL digits on the line. Draw a 1-cell-wide snake which moves orthogonally and does not touch itself (even diagonally). The snake must enter every 3x3 box exactly once and may not include any cell which is on a line (but may include circled cells). The snake acts as both a region sum line and a product sum line. A digit in a circle indicates the number of times that digit appears on the snake.
1794: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage cannot repeat and must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Digits in cells separated by a black dot have a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit is double the other).
1795: Normal sudoku rules apply. Assign each circle (dot) in the grid a digit from 1-9. If a digit N is assigned to a circle, that digit must be assigned to exactly N circles in the grid. Digits separated by a black circle have a ratio of 1:N, where N is the digit assigned to the circle. Digits separated by a white circle have a difference of N, where N is the digit assigned to the circle.
1796: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is partially covered in fog. Entering correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells, possibly revealing more clues. If an arrow is present in a cell, the digit in the cell the arrow comes from appears in the grid in the direction of the arrow at a distance of N cells, where N is the digit in the arrow's cell. Example: If R3C4 had an arrow pointing to the left and R3C4 was a 2, then the digit below that arrow (R4C4) would appear in R3C2 again. Each line in the grid is a palindrome. The sequence of digits along a palindrome read the same from both ends. Each palindrome is a single line in a unique color. Digits in cells that are connected by a white dot are consecutive. Digits in cells that are connected by a black dot are in a 1:2 ratio.
1797: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits an equal distance from the centre of a purple line must sum to the digit in the centre of that purple line.
1798: Normal sudoku rules apply. In each row, column and box there is exactly one 'pseudo cell.' The digits 1-9 each appear once in a pseudo cell. The real value of a pseudo cell (for the purposes of the coloured lines) is determined by multiplying its row number by its column number. Eg; if there is a pseudo cell in r6c3, it has the value of 18, regardless of which digit appears in that cell.
1799: Normal sudoku rules apply. Placing a correct digit in the grid will clear any fog in the surrounding cells. Lines are Renbans, German Whispers, or Region Sum Lines. The identity of each line must be deduced. Lines never cross or branch in this puzzle. Therefore, if two line segments enter the same cell, those line segments must be connected. Renbans are a sequence of non-repeating digits in any order. Along German Whispers adjacent digits on the line have a difference of at least 5. Region Sum Lines have the same sum in every 3x3 box they visit. If a Region Sum Line visits a box multiple times, each visit is counted as a separate sum. A dot between two digits means that those digits are either consecutive or have a 1:2 ratio. Not all dots are given.
1800: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat within a cage. The digits in each cage sum to an unknown total. A white dot between two cages indicates that the totals in those two cages have a difference of X. The value of X is the same for every white dot, but must be deduced.
1801: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into “galaxies”, which are orthogonally connected groups of cells that have 180 degree rotational symmetry about their centres, and do not overlap with other galaxies. All cells must be part of a galaxy. The centre of every galaxy is marked by a red dot. Digits may not repeat within a galaxy. No two adjacent cells in the grid (ie no domino) may have digits that are in a 1:2 ratio.
1802: Place the digits 1-9 once each in every row, column, and outlined region. There are three sets of clones in the grid, the locations of which must be determined. Each clone is a 3x3 square, and each set consists of three clones. Clones within the same set must contain identical digits in exactly the same positions. Rotations and reflections are not allowed. Clones do not overlap with other clones.
1803: Place the digits 1-9 once each in every row, column, and 9 cell orthogonally connected region. The location of each region must be determined. Along a thermometer, digits must increase from bulb to tip. The digit in the bulb of a thermometer indicates how many thermometer bulbs contain that digit. Additionally, the digit in the bulb of a thermometer indicates how many times that thermometer crosses a border between regions. A digit in a square indicates how many cells in its region are on a thermometer. A V shape between two digits points to the lower digit.
1804: Normal sudoku rules apply. Clues outside the grid are both Sandwich AND Skyscraper clues. As a sandwich, the clue gives the sum of the digits between 1 and 9 in that row or column. As a skyscraper, the clue represents how many digits would be visible when standing at the clue looking at its row or column, if each digit were a building with the height of its value. A "?" in a clue may represent any integer value. Digits along a thermometer must increase from bulb to tip. Digits on an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
1805: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end.
1806: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along a green line must have a difference of at least 5.
1807: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent values along a line must differ by at least 5. Nine cells in the grid are 'doublers', which count as double their value for the purpose of the lines. There is exactly one doubler in each row, column, and box, and they form a set of the digits 1-9.
1808: Normal Sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must not repeat and must sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. Digits separated by a white dot are consecutive. Not all dots are given. Draw a one-cell-wide loop of orthogonally connected cells. The loop may not touch itself, not even diagonally. The loop must enter every cell of every cage. The loop acts as a German Whispers line (i.e., adjacent digits on the loop must have a difference of at least 5). Additionally the grid is partially covered in fog. Placing correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells, possibly revealing more clues.
1809: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages cannot repeat and must sum to the small clue given in the upper left corner of the cage. Cells separated by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Not all dots are necessarily given. Draw a one-cell-wide loop of orthogonally connected cells. The loop may not touch itself, not even diagonally. The loop must occupy all cells of all given cages. Adjacent digits on the loop must alternate polarity (low [1234] vs high [6789]).
1810: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must not repeat and must sum to the number in the top left corner of the cage. Draw a one-cell-wide loop of orthogonally connected cells. The loop may not touch itself, not even diagonally. The loop must enter at least one cell of each cage. Numbers on the loop count as double their value when calculating cage sums. For example, a 2-cell cage summing to 10 may contain a 2 on the loop and a 6 not on the loop. The loop acts as a German Whispers line (i.e., adjacent digits on the loop must have a difference of at least 5). The original, undoubled value of the digit is always used for the purposes of the German Whispers constraint.
1811: Normal sudoku rules apply. Orthogonally connected cells of the same parity (odd vs. even) are parity islands. A digit in a circle indicates the size of the island that cell is in.
1812: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Cells separated by a black dot contain digits with a 2:1 ratio (ie one digit will be double the other). Not all possible dots are necessarily given. Digits in a circle must appear in at least one of the four surrounding cells. Draw a one-cell-wide loop of orthogonally connected cells. The loop may not touch itself, not even diagonally. The loop must enter exactly one of the four cells surrounding each given quad clue. The loop acts as a modular line. Each set of three adjacent digits along the loop must be one each from the sets [147], [258], and [369].
1813: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. Cells separated by an X must contain digits summing to 10; not all possible Xs are necessarily given. On either main diagonal (marked in blue) digits cannot repeat.
1814: Divide the grid into nine regions, each consisting of nine orthogonally-connected cells. Each row, column and region must contain the digits 1 to 9 once each. Each line must pass through at least two regions. A “line segment” consists of the digits along the line within a region from the point that line starts in that region to when it next leaves it (or ends). The sum of digits along each line segment along a line must be the same. Different lines can have different line segment totals. Digits in a circle indicate the number of cells that are part of a line in that cell's region.
1815: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each pair of circles of the same colour are connected by a hidden Between Line. Each Between Line may not branch, move diagonally, or take up a full 2x2 area. Separate Between Lines may not overlap. Cells along a Between Line must have values between those in the circles at the ends of that line.
1816: Normal sudoku rules apply. The dots given in the grid are the centres of rotationally symmetric “galaxies” (non-overlapping sets of orthogonally connected cells). Adjacent digits in the same galaxy must have a difference of at least 5. Caged cells are part of a galaxy with a given centre.
1817: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade the grid using two colours, such that all instances of each colour are orthogonally connected, and no 2x2 area is completely one colour. Blue lines must have an equal sum N within each colour they pass through. If a blue line passes through a colour multiple times, each individual pass sums to N. (N can be different for different lines). All lines must cross colours at least once. Cells separated by an X contain digits summing to 10.
1818: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid contains two “galaxies”. A galaxy is a collection of orthogonally-connected cells which exhibit 180 degree rotational symmetry around the central cell of the grid. Eg If r2c4 is in a galaxy then r8c6 must also be in that galaxy. All cells must be part of a galaxy and the two galaxies may only ever overlap in one cell - the central cell of the grid. No 2x2 area may be fully part of one galaxy. One of the galaxies is “redshifted” and cells in it have a value of one greater than their digit. The other galaxy is “blueshifted” and cells in it have a value of one less than their digit. Values along an arrow sum to the value in that arrow’s circle. Values in a cage sum to the given total. Digits may not repeat in a cage, but values may.
1819: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cells that are connected by a white dot are consecutive. Digits in cells that are connected by a black dot are in a 1:2 ratio. Digits along an arrow sum to the number in the attached circle.
