1820: Normal sudoku rules apply. Wherever a 2x2 area consists of two odd and two even digits in a checkerboard pattern, a little checkerboard symbol appears in its centre. If the symbol does not appear, the surrounding 2x2 does not have such a checkerboard pattern. Digits in cells that are an equal number of steps from the midpoint of a lavender line must sum to the digit on the midpoint (marked by a dot).
1821: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in the corresponding circle. Digits joined by an X sum to 10.
1822: The grid is covered in fog that hides cells underneath it. Placing correct digits will reveal surrounding cells. Construct nine non-overlapping 3x3 regions in the grid containing digits 1-9 once each. The rest of the grid must be left empty. Digits must not repeat along any row or column. Digits on a grey thermometer must strictly increase from the bulb-end. The sum of digits along a diagonal indicated by a clue outside the grid must satisfy either the given inequality or the corresponding relationship with other such clues.
1823: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a pink “renban” form a set of non-repeating, consecutive digits in any order. Digits do not repeat along gold “nabner” lines. Additionally, no two digits appearing anywhere on a nabner line can be consecutive. Eg If a line contains a 2, there cannot be a 1 or 3 anywhere along the line. Adjacent digits along a green line must differ in value by at least 5. Box borders divide the blue line into segments with the same sum.
1824: Place 1-9 in each row, column and marked region. Digits on a wide purple Renban line form a set of consecutive digits in any order. Digits on a thin blue region sum line have the same total for each region the line enters. Different lines may have different totals. Digits on a gold Nabner line may not repeat - if a digit appears on the line then digits consecutive with it must not appear on that line at all.
1825: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in the quad circles must appear in the surrounding four cells. Digits in some quads must be deduced. The white segments represent 'Difference Fences'. Each segment has a value equal to the difference between the cells they separate. On a fence, no two segments can have the same value. Each fence has a total value equal to the sum of all the segments on the fence and this total value is given in the attached quad (it may be a 2-digit number). Some total values will need to be deduced.
1826: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a thermometer, digits increase from bulb to tip. Digits along an orange arrow average exactly to the digit in that arrow's circle. Multiple arrows extending from the same circle are treated as different arrows each averaging to the circled digit. For example, a circled 3 could have 15 on one of its arrows, and 24 on the other, because both arrows would average to 3. For clarity, 'average' in this puzzle refers to the arithmetic mean.
1827: Normal sudoku rules apply. The digits within a cage must sum to the small clue in the top-left corner of that cage. The inequality sign points to the smaller digit.
1828: Normal sudoku rules apply. Box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum. Neighbouring digits on the green line have a difference of at least 5. Digits joined by an X sum to 10. Digits joined by a V sum to 5. Not all Xs and Vs are given. Digits joined by a white dot are consecutive. Not all dots are given.
1829: Normal sudoku rules apply. An X connects two digits that sum to 10. Not all possible Xs are given. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Along a green line, adjacent digits have the difference of at least 5. Along a pink line, digits form a set of non-repeating consecutive digits that can be in any order.
1830: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a white dot must be consecutive (not all dots are given). A digit in a grey square must be even. Each cell containing a circle is the head of a parity snake, whose length is the digit in the circle. A parity snake is a non-branching one-cell-wide path of orthogonally connected cells of the same parity, which may not orthogonally touch itself or other cells of matching parity. A snake may not have two heads, and may be a single cell.
1831: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a line sum to the product of the digits in the squares at either end of the line (NB If it is the same square (eg r8c8) multiply that digit with itself). The sum does not include the digits in the squares. Digits may repeat on a line if permitted by the other rules.
1832: Normal sudoku rules apply. Most of the grid is obscured by fog. Placing a correct digit will remove the fog surrounding that cell. Each letter from A-J uniquely represents one of the digits 0-9. A two-letter clue represents a two-digit number which does not begin with 0. A clue outside the grid represents the sum of the digits in the first X cells seen from that clue, where X is the first cell seen. (Eg if r1c5 is a 5 then the IF clue is summing the first 5 cells in its column.) Digits in a cage do not repeat and sum to the cage total, which is given in the leftmost cell of the highest row of the cage.
1833: Normal sudoku rules apply. All lines are both Renban AND Zipper lines. Centres of Zipper lines are marked by small circles. Renban lines use a set of non-repeating consecutive digits in some order. Along Zipper lines, pairs of digits equidistant from the center have the same sum. For odd length Zipper lines, that sum is the value in the center cell of the line.
1834: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into 3 orthogonally connected sections such that each pair of sections shares an edge and no 2x2 square in the grid belongs to a single section. A digit in a circle indicates the number of circles in its section. On section-sum lines, all adjacent groups of digits along the line which are part of the same section have the same sum. No line can be entirely in one section.
1835: Place the digits 1-9, once each, in every row, column and marked region. When digit z is in cell (x, y) then digit y is in cell (x, z) and digit x is in cell (z, y).
1836: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells a knight's move apart cannot contain the same digit. A purple line contains a non-repeating set of consecutive digits in any order. The sum of the digits in two orange circles is equal to the sum of the digits along the line joining them. The word Agadmator appears along the diagonal of the grid. Each instance of a given letter represents the same digit, and no two different letters represent the same digit. The M positioned on a corner is the difference between R6C6 and R7C7.
1837: Normal sudoku rules apply. Box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum. Cells separated by a black dot must contain digits with a ratio of 1:2. Not all dots are given.
1838: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw in lines that move orthogonally from cell to cell. Two circles of the same colour are start and end of a line. Lines may not intersect themselves or other lines. The lines drawn in the grid act both as a Region Sum Line (RSL) and a Modular Line (ML). Additionally, digits CANNOT repeat on a line. Region Sum Line: Along a RSL line, box borders divide the line into segments with the same sum. Every set of three sequential digits along a ML must contain a complete set of residues modulo 3, i.e. one digit from {1,4,7}, one from {2,5,8}, and one from {3,6,9}.
1839: Normal sudoku rules apply. It must be determined whether each white dot is a kropki dot or the centre of a galaxy. The two digits joined by a white kropki dot have a difference indicated by the number on the kropki dot. A galaxy is a group of orthogonally connected cells, that has the white dot at its centre and is rotationally symmetrical through 180 degrees. The number on the central dot of a galaxy indicates the number of cells (N) in the galaxy. This galaxy must contain all the digits from 1 to N. Galaxies also function like region sum lines; digits within each 3x3 box sum to the same amount if they are within the same galaxy. This region sum may be different for different galaxies. Galaxies cannot share cells with any other galaxies or cells joined by a kropki dot.
1840: Normal sudoku rules apply. A clue outside the grid gives the sum of the digits along the indicated diagonal. Digits separated by a black dot are in a 1:2 ratio. Gray lines are palindromes that read the same in both directions. Digits cannot repeat along the marked diagonal.
1841: Fill the grid with the numbers 1-7 such that no number repeats in a row or column. The grid is completely covered by thermometer lines. You cannot see them because they are invisible. Nevertheless, numbers increase along thermometers starting from their bulb end. Thermometer lines move orthogonally and diagonally, and do not cross themselves or other thermometers, except at the white diamonds, where they must cross themselves or another thermometer. Thermometers do not pass through Xs. Thermometer bulbs do not touch each other, even diagonally. All thermometers have the same length.
1842: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the number in the cell pointed at by the cage's northwest corner. Digits cannot repeat in a cage. eg: row 1 column 2 shows the sum of the grid’s upper-leftmost cage. A cell with an arrow shows the sum of the digits on the arrow's diagonal.
1843: Normal sudoku rules apply. Fog covers the grid. Correctly placing digits clears the fog. A black dot in a cell indicates its value has a 2-to-1 ratio with that of some neighbor (where "neighbor" means a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell). A white dot in a cell indicates its value is adjacent to the value of some neighbor. A grey dot in a cell indicates that its value and some neighbor's value sum to 5. All possible dots have been given, but some dots may be hiding behind other dots.

1846: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the number in its corner. Cells that half-appear in a cage only contribute half their value to its sum. Digits appear at most once in the same cage (but half-appearing twice counts as appearing once!).
1847: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage do not repeat and sum to the small clue in the top left corner of the cage. On each of the marked diagonals digits do not repeat.
1848: Normal sudoku rules apply. A clue outside the grid indicates the value of the sum of all even or all odd digits on the indicated diagonal. 1849: Normal sudoku rules apply. All cages are minmax killer cages. Digits in a minmax killer cage do not repeat. The clue in the top left indicates the sum of the smallest and the largest digit that are contained in the cage. 1850: Normal sudoku rules apply. All given cages are “divisor killer cages”. Digits in a divisor killer cage do not repeat. 1851: Normal irregular 7x7 Sudoku rules apply, i.e. each row, column and region must contain the digits from 1 to 7 once each. All cages are “Rellik Cages”. 1852: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage do not repeat and sum to the clue in the top left.
1853: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits connected by an X or V sum to 10 or 5, respectively. Not every X and V is given. Each pink line contains a set of consecutive, non-repeating digits, in any order.
1854: Normal sudoku rules apply. The digits in each 2x2-square that crosses at least one box border sum to a multiple of eight - except for the square marked in grey. The digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle.
1855: Divide the grid into 9 kingdoms of orthogonally connected cells. Fill the grid with the digits 1-9 so that each digit appears once in each row, column and kingdom. A digit on a castle indicates exactly how many castles contain that digit. Every kingdom has a score, representing how powerful it is. This is calculated by adding the number of castles the kingdom contains to the number of neighbouring kingdoms it borders. (Two kingdoms are considered neighbours if they share at least one orthogonal edge.) A digit in a blue square indicates its kingdom's score. No two kingdoms have the same score. A bridge connects two digits in different kingdoms, and they will either sum to 5, sum to 10, or be in a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit will be double the other).
1856: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat on the indicated diagonal. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Clues outside the grid give the sum of the digits along the indicated diagonal. Digits in cells with a shaded square must be even.
1857: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along each line have values which lie between those of the digits in the circles at either end of that line. Moreover, for the three brown lines, the digit in one of the circles is the sum of the remaining digits including the digit in the other circle.
1858: Normal sudoku rules apply. The value of a digit inside the black dot (i.e. box 5) is double its normal value. 1863: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along a green line have a difference of at least five.

1865: Normal sudoku rules apply. Whites live between digits with consecutive values. Blacks live between digits in a 2:1 ratio. Not all possible dots are given. 1866: Normal Sudoku rules apply Kings are 1s, Rooks are 2s, Bishops are 3s, Knights are 4s. Basically, no King can be "in check". 1867: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end. Kings are 1, Rooks are 2, Bishops are 3, Knights are 4. No King can be “in check”. 1869: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells an equal distance from the center of the Zipper lines must sum to the cell in the center of the line. Two separate straight lines pass through r5c5. Digits in cages must sum to the number in the corner of the cage.
1870: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat in cages which sum to the total shown. Digits along a Sapho Juice colored thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Digits in cells separated by a black dot must be in a 2:1 ratio.
1871: Normal sudoku rules apply. Neighbouring digits along a Green Champagne Flute differ by at least 5. Neighbouring digits along an Orange Champagne Flute Line differ by at least 4. 1873: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers inside a BLUE low pressure gauge indicate how many digits STRICTLY GREATER than that number appear in the up to 8 cells surrounding the gauge. 1874: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along arrows sum to the digit in the attached circle. Clues outside the grid show the sum of the indicated diagonal. Digits can repeat on arrows and diagonals.
1875: Normal sudoku rules apply. The cage shows its sum. Digits next to each other on a line have a difference of at least 5.
1876: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Digits in circles also show the total number of cells of the same even/odd parity that that cell sees horizontally and vertically (including itself) before it hits a cell with another parity.
1877: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells separated by a knight's move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit. In each cage, digits cannot repeat and must sum to 10.
1878: Normal sudoku rules apply. A number outside the grid indicates the sum of digits between the 1 and the 9 in that row or column. 1885: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in the attached circle. Cages show their sums.
1886: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat along the marked diagonal. 1887: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in the attached circle. Arrows do not branch or overlap. 1889: 11x11 deconstruction rules apply: fill the grid with nine non-overlapping 3x3 square regions, such that each region contains the digits 1-9 once each and no digit repeats in any row or column. Cells outside regions do not contain digits. All cells that contain digits form a single orthogonally-connected region. All cells that do not contain digits form a loop that is one cell wide and does not branch or touch itself, even diagonally. The following standard clues appear in the puzzle: Thermometers: digits on thermometers increase from the bulb. Region sum lines: box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum. Renban lines: purple lines contain a non-repeating set of consecutive digits in any order. Nabner lines: gold lines contain a non-repeating set of digits, and no two digits on the same line can be consecutive (regardless of their position on the line). Digits in cells with a shaded square must be even. Digits in cells with a shaded circle must be odd. However, all clues are wrogn! For the purposes of this puzzle: A thermometer is not “wrogn” if any cell on the thermometer contains a digit that is equal to or less than a digit in a cell that is further from the bulb. A region sum line is not “wrogn” if any two segments (as divided by box borders) on the same line contain a set of digits that sum to the same number. A renban line is not “wrogn” if, for any digit N that appears on the line, another digit on the line is equal to N, N–1, or N+1. A nabner line is not “wrogn” unless all of the following conditions are true: - the smallest digit on the line is consecutive with exactly one other digit on the same line, - the largest digit on the line is consecutive with exactly one other digit on the same line, and - all other digits on the line are consecutive with exactly two other digits on the same line. A cell with a shaded square is not “wrogn” if it contains an even digit. A cell with a shaded circle is not “wrogn” if it contains an odd digit. For each of the clues above, cells that do not contain digits are ignored. In addition, exactly one of the following chess-based constraints applies: Anti-bishop: cells separated by a bishop’s move cannot contain the same digit. Anti-king: cells separated by a king’s move cannot contain the same digit. Anti-knight: cells separated by a knight’s move cannot contain the same digit. Anti-rook: cells separated by a rook’s move cannot contain the same digit.
1890: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into regions of orthogonally connected cells. Two regions of the same size may not share an edge. Each region must contain at least one circle. 1891: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits a (chess) king's move apart must be different. Adjacent digits on a green line differ by at least 5. Box borders divide a blue line into segments with the same sum. Black dot digits are in a 1:2 ratio, white dot digits are consecutive.
1892: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the total in the top left corner (if given). Digits cannot repeat within a cage.
1893: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Draw a one-cell-wide loop of orthogonally connected cells. The loop may not touch itself, not even diagonally. Digits on the loop count as double their value for the purposes of arrows/circles.
1894: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on the red line must differ by at least 5. 1895: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells with grey squares contain even digits. On the purple lines, any two cells an equal distance from their centre cell must sum to the digit in that centre cell.
1896: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the indicated total. Cells that half-appear in a cage only contribute half their value to its sum. Cells that quarter-appear in a cage only contribute a quarter of their value to its sum. Digits appear at most once in the same cage (half-appearing twice counts as appearing once).
1897: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a thermo increase from the bulb to the tip.
1898: Every row, column and 3x3 box contains the digits 0-9 once each. To enable this, one cell in each row, column, and 3x3 box is a Schrödinger cell (S-Cell) ie it contains two digits. 1899: Normal sudoku deconstruction rules apply. ie Fill the grid with nine non-overlapping 3x3 square regions, such that each region contains the digits 1-9 once each and no digit repeats in any row or column. Cells outside regions do not contain digits. Along thermometers, digits increase from the bulb end.
1900: Normalish sudoku rules apply : Put the digits 0-9 into each row column and box once each. In order to allow this, each row, column, and box will have one "Schreedinger-cell" which contains exactly 3 digits. The value of any "Schreedinger-cell" is the sum of its 3 digits. This will affect the arithmetic on arrows, renbans, german whispers and kropki dots. Arrows: the values of cells along an arrow sum to the value in that arrow's circle. Renban: the values of cells on a renban (purple) line form a set of non-repeating consecutive numbers in any order. German Whispers: the values of cells along a green line must differ by at least 5. Quadruples: the digits contained in the small white circles must each appear at least once in the 4 surrounding cells. Kropki: black dots separate cells whose values have a 1:2 ratio. 1901: Normalish sudoku rules apply: Every row column and 3x3 box contains the digits 0-9 once each. To enable this, one cell in each row, column, and box is a Schrödinger cell (S-Cell): it contains two digits. For the purpose of the other rules, the value of an S-cell is the sum of its 2 digits. The values of the digits contained in the small white circles must each appear at least once in the 4 surrounding cells. For example, at least 3 of the 4 cells around the circle in R89C67 must have a value of 6. Blue lines must have an equal sum N within each 3x3 box they pass through. Eg r1c3+r2c3=r1c4+r1c5+r1c6=r1c7+r2c7. If a line re-enters a 3x3 box, each segment sums to N separately. Different lines may have different values for N.
1902: Normal sudoku rules apply. The values of the cells in a cage must sum to the small clue in the top left corner pf the cage. Digits may not repeat in cages (but values may repeat). In every row, column and 3x3 box, is a “mirrored digit”. It takes the value opposite to its own value on the 1-9 scale. (In other words, 1 takes the value of 9, 2 the value of 8... 9 the value of 1.) Each digit 1-9 is mirrored once.
1903: Fill the grid with 9 non-overlapping 3x3 square regions, such that each region contains the digits 1-9 once each and no digit repeats in any row or column. Cells outside regions do not contain digits. The whole 11x11 grid must form a valid “yin yang” grid: ie shade some cells such that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected, all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected, and no 2x2 area is fully shaded or fully unshaded. Digits in a cage must not repeat. The number in the top left corner indicates either the sum of the digits of the shaded cells or the sum of the digits of the unshaded cells contained within that cage.
1904: Normal sudoku rules apply. In this puzzle, each digit from 1-9 is represented by a letter from A-I. You must determine which letter represents which digit. When discovered, these can be entered into the orange boxes at the bottom. The 2x2 area surrounding a quad circle must contain all the digits represented by the letters in that circle. The digits along a grey line can be divided into one or more non-overlapping groups of adjacent cells, each of which sums to 10. The digits in a blue or yellow cage must sum to the total in the top left corner. Enter correct digits near the grey fog cells to clear the fog. No guessing is necessary.
1905: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat within a cage. Cage clues show the sum of the digits in that cage, rounded to the nearest multiple of 5.
1906: Fill the grid with the digits 1-6 so that each digit appears once in each row, column and region. The orange clues are X products: they give the product of the first X digits in the indicated direction, where X is the first digit seen in that direction. Each question mark represents a digit of the clue. These may be any digit from 0-9. All clues must be determined. Also, every digit represented by a question mark indicates exactly how many times that digit is being represented by a question mark, eg: if a clue contains a 5, then exactly 5 of the question marks are a 5.
1907: Normal 6x6 sudoku rules apply. Each digit in a circle indicates how many times that digit appears in a circle in the puzzle. Digits strictly never appear more than once in a cage. Cells separated by an X sum to 10. Not all possible Xs are given. Grey lines are palindromes, i.e. digits equidistant from a grey line's center are always the same. Those are all the rules. Do not forget any of them.
1908: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers in circles are simultaneously skyscraper sums, full rank clues, and arrow bulbs. SKYSCRAPER SUMS: imagine each cell as a building of height N, where N is the digit in the cell. A clue outside the grid gives the sum of heights of buildings that can be seen in that row or column, whereby larger buildings obscure the view of smaller ones, eg the row 415798362 has a skyscraper sum of 4+5+7+9=25 from the left and 2+6+8+9=25 from the right. FULL RANK: imagine each row and column, read in either direction, as a 9-digit number. If all 36 such numbers were listed in ascending order, then the clue indicates the rank which the corresponding row/column would take in that list. ARROW BULBS give the sum of the digits along the attached arrow. Digits may repeat on arrows if permitted by other sudoku rules. Arrow shafts in R4C6 cross each other; they do not bend.
1909: Normal sudoku rules apply. The digit on one endpoint of a blue line indicates the total number of even digits on the line while the digit on the other end indicates the total number of odd digits on the line. These totals include the digits on the endpoints. A white dot between two cells means that the values of those cells must be consecutive. Not all dots are necessarily given.
1910: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages cannot repeat and sum to the value shown. Along a Zipper line, pairs of digits equidistant from the center of the line have the same sum. For Zipper lines of odd length, that sum is the central digit on the line.
1911: Fill the grid with the digits 1–9 so that no digit repeats in a row, column, or 3x3 region. The red dashed lines indicate the boundaries of regions, and cells on the lines are simultaneously part of the regions on both sides of the line. Cells that are a knight's move apart (in chess) cannot contain the same digit. Digits in a cage cannot repeat and must sum to the given total.
1912: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Digits cannot repeat within a cage. Cells separated by a white dot contain consecutive digits. Cells separated by a black dot contain digits in a 1:2 ratio (ie one digit will be double the other). Not all possible dots are given.
1913: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end; however the digit 1 may be considered as having the value of 1 or 10.
1914: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the value in its circle. There are 9 Vampire cells contained within the grid which are a set of the digits from 1-to-9. Each row, column and box contains exactly one Vampire cell. 9 Prey cells in the grid follow the same rules as the Vampire cells. A cell may have only one of these roles. For Arrows/Circles: Prey cells contribute no value; Vampire cells contribute the sum of the digits in the Vampire cell and the Prey cell within the same box.
1915: Normal sudoku rules apply. The value of digits within a cage must sum to the small clue in the top-left corner of the cage. Digits must not repeat within a cage (but values may repeat). The value of digits along a thermometer must increase from the bulb to the tip. There are 9 Hot cells contained within the grid comprised of a set of the digits 1-to-9. Each row, column and box contains exactly one Hot cell. There are nine 9 Cold cells contained within the grid following the same rules as the Hot cells. A cell may have only one of these roles. For cages and thermometer values, Hot cells increase the value of the contained digit by 1; and Cold cells decrease the value of the contained digit by 1.
1916: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each of the following standard clue types occurs exactly three times in the grid: Arrow, Circle, Dots, Odd/Even, X/V and Zipper . For each of those clue types, exactly two of the appearances of that clue are correct and the other is incorrect. The "standard" clue types mentioned above are as follows: White dots: Cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive digits. Black dots: Cells separated by a black dot must be in the ratio of 1:2 (so one digit must be double the other). Arrow: Digits on an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow's grey circle. Xs: Cells separated by an X must contain digits summing to 10. Vs: Cells separated by a V must contain digits summing to 5. Odds: Cells containing an opaque grey circle must contain an odd digit. Evens: Cells containing an opaque grey square must contain an even digit. Circle: A digit in a purple circle indicates exactly how many purple circles contain that digit. Zipper: digits an equal distance from the centre of a blue line must sum to the digit in the middle of that line.
1917: Place the digits 0 through 9 once each in every row, column and box; to enable this, each row, column and box contains exactly one Schrödinger Cell ie a cell that contains two digits. The grid is partially covered in fog; placing correct digits in non-Schrödinger cells will clear the fog from the surrounding area (no guessing is required). Each of the standard clue types below occurs exactly three times in the grid; for each, exactly two of the appearances of that clue are correct and the other is incorrect. The clue types are: - Counting Circles (ie each circled digit counts exactly how many circles contain that digit. All other clue types consider the sum total of a cell as that cell’s value.); - Dutch Whisper - adjacent cells along an orange line must differ in value by at least 4; - German Whisper – adjacent cells along a green line must differ in value by at least 5; - Killer cages - values in a killer cage must sum to small clue in the top left corner of the cage & digits cannot repeat in a cage; - Kropki dots ie cells separated by a white dot must contain consecutive values & cells separated by a black dot must contain values in a 1:2 ratio (ie one value is double the other); and - X/V rules ie cells separated by an X must contain values summing to 10 and cells separated by a V must contain values summing to 5.
1918: Normal sudoku rules apply. White dots separate two cells containing consecutive values; Black dots separate two cells where one value is double the other [1:2]. Values along a purple Renban line form a set of consecutive, non-repeating values in any order. Values along a yellow Nabner line form a set of non-consecutive, non-repeating values in any order (e.g. if a cell of value 3 appears on a Nabner line, then values of 2 and 4 cannot appear). There are 9 Hot cells contained within the grid comprising a set of the digits from 1 to 9. Each row, column and box contains exactly one Hot cell. There are nine 9 Cold cells contained within the grid following the same rules as the Hot cells. A cell may have only one of these roles. Hot cells increase the value of the contained digit by 1. Cold cells decrease the value of the contained digit by 1.
1919: Normal sudoku rules apply. Any two orthogonally adjacent cells cannot contain digits in a 1:2, 1:3, 1:4 or 1:5 ratio. Every horizontal set of three orthogonally connected cells within any 3x3 box is a modular sequence (i.e. must contain one digit from [1 4 7], one digit from [2 5 8] and one digit from [3 6 9]). Every vertical set of three orthogonally connected cells within any 3x3 box is an entropic sequence (i.e. must contain one digit from [1 2 3], one digit from [4 5 6] and one digit from [7 8 9]). There are no 3's in a corner of the grid.
1920: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat on a marked diagonal. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in the attached circle.
1921: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along thermometers, digits must increase from the bulb end. Digits on between lines must be between the digits in the attached circles. Adjacent digits along the green wheel (line) must differ by at least 5. Digits along a purple line are a set of consecutive, non-repeating digits in any order. Lines go straight where they cross. Digits separated by a white dot must be consecutive. Digits separated by an X must sum to 10.
1922: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in thick bordered squares must be equal to the square root of the 2-digit number read from top to bottom in the corresponding cage. All squares must contain a different digit. Every square root sign also represents a different constraint. Parity line (red): Adjacent digits along the red line must alternate in parity (odd/even). Entropic line (orange): A set of three sequential cells along the orange line must contain a low [123], middle [456], and high [789] digit. German Whisper line (green): Adjacent digits along the green line must differ by at least 5. Renban (purple): Digits along the purple line are a set of consecutive, non-repeating digits in any order. Region Sum line (blue): Along a blue line, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total. Thermometer (grey): Digits along the thermometer must increase from the bulb to the tip (which are always at the ends of the line); which end is the bulb and which the tip must be deduced.
1923: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat on a marked diagonal. Digits separated by a white dot must be consecutive. Digits separated by a black dot must be in a 1:2 ratio.
1924: Normal sudoku rules apply. All thermometers are slow thermometers, as well as region sum lines. ie Digits along these thermometers must either stay the same or increase from the bulb end; and box borders divide each blue line into segments with the same sum. eg r8c2 + r7c3 = r6c4. Digits separated by a white dot must be consecutive. Not all dots are given.
1925: Normal sudoku rules apply. A clue outside the grid has TWO functions: X-Sums, which sum the first X digits from the clue in its row/column, where X is the first digit seen; and Little Killer, where the clue gives the sum of the indicated diagonal.
1926: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along grey lines between two circles must have values between those circles. Adjacent digits on a green line differ by 5 or more. Cells separated by the white dot must be consecutive. Cells separated by the black dot have a 1:2 ratio. The inequality sign points to the smaller cell.
1927: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along a green line must differ by at least 5. A digit in column 1 indicates the column in which the digit 1 appears in that row. Columns 5 and 9 have the same rule for the digits 5 and 9 respectively. (For example, an 8 in R7C1 tells you there's a 1 in R7C8. A 3 in R2C5 tells you there's a 5 in R2C3.)
1928: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages sum to the clue in the corner of the cage. Adjacent digits on the red ring have different parity (odd/even). Adjacent digits on the green ring differ by at least 5. Digits on the blue line sum to the same value in each region the ring passes through.
1929: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits inside a cage do not repeat and sum to the small clue in the corner of the cage. All cages additionally act as fortresses – each digit inside a cage is greater than its orthogonally adjacent neighbors outside the cage.
1930: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on a thermometer increase from bulb to tip. The orange circle contains an odd digit. No orthogonally adjacent pair of digits sums to 10.
1931: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a line must be strictly increasing in one direction or the other. Digits separated by the white dot are consecutive. Digits separated by the black dot are in a 2:1 ratio.
1932: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. Along a marked diagonal, digits cannot repeat. Cells separated by a single knight’s move (in chess) cannot contain the same digit.
1933: Normal sudoku rules apply. Construct a one-cell-wide snake of orthogonally-connected cells whose two endpoints are given as circles. The snake cannot branch and cannot touch itself orthogonally, but may touch itself diagonally. Additionally: All squares are on the snake; a digit in a square gives the number of snake cells seen in all horizontal/vertical directions combined, including the cell with the square - non-snake cells block the vision; the snake acts as a “German Whisper” line ie adjacent digits on the snake must have a difference of at least 5.
1934: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must sum to the given total. Octopus rules apply. I.e. draw 4 lines that must each: i) not cross or overlap anywhere except r5c5, where they all intersect; ii) have 180-degree rotational symmetry around r5c5; iii) visit exactly 2 cells on the edge of the grid, which are the beginning and end of the line; and iv) all be the same length (in number of cells passed through). The 4 lines are "Same Difference" lines. I.e pairs of adjacent digits on a line must all have the same difference, though this difference may be different for different lines.
1935: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells so that the unshaded cells form a single orthogonally connected area, and each connected shaded region touches the grid boundary. A circle is always unshaded, and the digit in the circle equals the number of unshaded cells visible in a straight line from that cell, including the cell itself. Shaded cells obstruct the view. Each shaded region contains a corner clue which equals the sum of the digits in that region. Digits may not repeat in a shaded region, and the digit in the clued cell equals the size of the region.
1936: Normal sudoku rules apply. Two 2s, four 4s and five 5s are considered to have double their value, for the purposes of the following clues. Digits must not repeat in cages, and the total sum of all values in the cage is given by the small number. Digits along a purple line must form a set of consecutive non-repeating values. Values along an arrow sum to the value in the attached circle.
1937: Place one or more digits from 1-9 in every cell so that each digit appears exactly once in every row, column, and 3x3 box. All the digits in the cell(s) touching each V sum to 5. White dots always separate a pair of adjacent digits (but there can also be additional digits in the separated cells).
1938: Normal sudoku rules apply. (ie place the digits 1-9, once each, in every row, column & 3x3 box). A digit in a circle indicates how many circles contain that digit. Place some circles in the grid such that a box “m” contains exactly “m” number of circles. (Boxes are numbered in normal reading order so the top left box of the grid is box 1, the bottom right box is box 9, etc). ie Box 1 should have 1 circle; box 3 should have 3 circles; etc. If a cell, eg R1C1, contains a circle then all the cells beneath it in the grid (8 cells in this case) must contain circles. No two 9s in the grid can be separated by a single Chess King’s or single Chess Knight’s move; but every 9 must share a diagonal with at least one other 9.
1939: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits cannot repeat inside a cage. Digits in a white circle must appear at least once each in the four surrounding cells. Digits on a line must have the same sum as the sum of the circles on the line's ends.
1940: Digits 1-5 appear in each marked region. No digit can be within a (chess) king's move of an identical digit. No orthogonal or diagonal trio of adjacent digits is an arithmetical sequence in order. So e.g. 123, 531 or 345 are forbidden but e.g. 132, 513 and 245 are allowed.
1941: Normal Sudoku rules apply. PARROTY LINES: A 'word' is a non-repeating sequence of digits, like '365', '24', or '7' (but not '747'). Each white Parroty Line consists of one or more copies of the same word. The digit on a parrot indicates the length of the word the parrot is saying. (Example: a parrot with a 3 could be saying “486 486”). Digits in a cage sum to the attached tag.
1942: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat in a cage, and each cage sums to one of four distinct totals, which must be determined. Cages that share an edge must have different sums, and no digit may appear in more than one cage with the same sum.
1943: Normal sudoku rules apply. Draw a snake (a one-cell wide path) into the grid which does not touch itself orthogonally. Areas not covered by the snake form 8 separate regions, one of each size 1-8 ('eggs') which, in turn, may touch one another diagonally but not orthogonally. Adjacent cells on a green line must contain one snake cell and one egg cell AND these cells’ digits must differ in value by at least 5. If a circle is in an egg, it gives the count of cells in the egg. If a circle is on the snake, it gives the number of snake cells “seen” by that circle, including itself (ie the number of contiguous snake cells extending horizontally and vertically from that cell, including itself).
1944: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along an orange line have a difference of at least four. The small numbers in each cage show the sum of the digits in the cage and digits cannot repeat in a cage.
1945: Fill the cells with the digits 1 to 8 such that each digit appears exactly once in every row, column and region. A region is a collection of eight orthogonally connected cells. Determining the shape of the regions is part of the puzzle. Each region has exactly one clue which is a small number in the upper left corner of some cell in that region (not necessarily the top left cell). Shade some cells such that: a) no orthogonally neighboring cells are shaded across a region boundary; b) all shaded cells within a region are orthogonally connected; an c) the digits in all shaded cells within a region sum to the region's clue. If all of the shaded groups were to fall straight down without changing shape, they must completely fill the bottom half of the grid.
1946: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits separated by a white Kropki dot must be consecutive. Digits separated by a black Kropki dot must have a ratio of 1:2. Sets of digits separated by a white Kroopki ‘doot’ (the long, ellipse-looking things) must have their respective sums be consecutive. Sets of digits separated by a black Kroopki doot must have their respective sums be in a 1:2 ratio.
1947: Fillomino: Divide the grid into regions of orthogonally-connected cells such that no two regions of the same size (ie with the same number of cells) share an edge. Enter a number into each cell equal to the size of its region. Four Colour Theorem: Each region must be shaded entirely in one colour. There are a total of four different colours in the grid. Regions of the same colour cannot touch orthogonally. Additionally, regions of the same colour must be of different sizes. Arrows: Digits on arrows indicate the distance to the nearest cell of the same colour in the indicated direction (Adjacent cells are a distance of 1 from each other). Not all arrows are necessarily given.
1948: Fillomino: Divide the grid into regions of orthogonally-connected cells such that no two regions of the same size share an edge. Enter a number into each cell equal to the size of its region. Look-and-Say Cages: Digits can repeat in cages. The number in the top left corner should be read as a look-and-say number and says which digits are in that cage. For example, if a cage has the clue "12" then it means there is one 2 in the cage. If it has the clue "3314" then it means there are three 3s and one 4 in the cage.
1949: The entire grid is comprised of an inner 9x9 grid and the areas (of non-black cells) where outside clues are to be placed by the solver. Divide the entire grid into regions of orthogonally-connected cells such that no two regions of the same size share an edge. Enter a number into each cell equal to the size of its region (ie the number of cells it contains). Regions can contain cells from both the inner 9x9 grid and the outside area. Numbers outside the 9x9 grid are valid “Numbered Rooms” clues. Ie A clue indicates the number that appears in the Nth cell of the clue's direction (inside the 9x9 grid) where N is the digit next to the clue in that direction.
1950: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in tabs must be placed within three cells of the narrow end of the tab (in that direction) in that row or column. A purple line contains a set of consecutive digits, in any order.
1951: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Purple “renban” lines contain a non-repeating set of consecutive digits in any order. Gold “nabner” lines contain a non-repeating set of digits, and no two digits on the same line can be consecutive (regardless of their position on the line). Along orange “entropic” lines, every set of three adjacent cells must contain one low digit (1-3), one middle digit (4-6), and one high digit (7-9). Digits in cells separated by an X sum to 10. Digits in cells with a shaded square must be even.
1952: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a purple line form a sequence of consecutive numbers in any order. Adjacent numbers on a green line must have a difference of at least 5. Digits cannot repat in a cage and sum to the number given.
1953: Normal sudoku rules apply. Within a cage, digits do not repeat and sum to the total given.
1954: Place the digits from 1 to 8 exactly once in every row, column, and region. Each region consists of eight orthogonally connected cells and must be located by the solver. A cell with an arrow (or arrows) indicates how many cells in the indicated directions combined do NOT belong to the same region as that cell.
1955: A murder has been committed in Grid Mansion! Dr Awkward has been found dead, and there are six suspects. Can you work out who did it? Normal sudoku rules apply: place the digits 1-9 once each in every row, column, and 3x3 room. FIND YOUR PATH: • Draw a line passing through the centres of some cells to represent your journey from room to room, as you interrogate suspects and look for clues. • Your path must start at one of the lettered cells (these are initials labelling the six suspects and the victim.) The path must finish at another lettered cell, and visit all the other lettered cells along the way. • Your path may move orthogonally or diagonally between cells, but may not cross itself. • You may not pass through a thick black wall; you can only get from room to room by travelling through the CENTRE of a doorway. For some doorways this may mean you have to go through diagonally. • The value of digits along your path must constantly increase or stay the same (like a slow thermometer). You must never move from a higher value to a lower value. PSEUDO CELLS: • Every row, column and room has exactly one 'pseudo cell'. These 9 pseudo cells contain the digits 1-9 once each.• For the purposes of your path, and for the weapon, victim and suspect rules below, the value of a pseudo cell equals its room number (regardless of which digit appears in the cell.) Rooms are numbered from 1-9 in reading order. Eg: room 1 is in the top left, room 7 is in the bottom left. WEAPONS: • Some weapons have been found, at locations marked by an X. The values of the two cells separated by a weapon sum to 10. THE VICTIM: • Dr Awkward's body was found lying awkwardly in the doorway between rooms 4 and 7. This has been marked by a white outline. All that's known about the victim is that the values of his cells form a palindrome, reading the same from either end. THE SUSPECTS: • Digits do not repeat in a killer cage (although their values might.) Each suspect has a particular trait: • Miss Parity (red) - values of orthogonally adjacent cell have a different parity (one is odd, the other is even). • Mrs Summer (blue) - a doorway divides her cells into two distinct groups, whose values both have the same sum. • Miss Tenclumpz - (white) - her cells can be divided into smaller distinct groups of orthogonally connected cells, each of which sum to 10. • Colonel Nabner (yellow) - none of his cell's values are consecutive with (or the same as) each other. • Professor Zipworthy (purple) - cells an equal distance from his central spot sum to the digit on his central spot. • The Whispering Reverend (green) - adjacent cells must have values with a difference of at least 5. One particular digit (not value) appears in all of the suspects' cages, except for the real killer. Who is it?
1956: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells so that every orthogonally connected group of shaded cells is rectangular, and every orthogonally connected group of unshaded cells is non-rectangular. (For the avoidance of doubt, a square is a rectangle.) A digit in a circle represents the number of cells in its shaded or unshaded group. Clues above a column represent the sum of any SHADED cells between the 1 and 9 in that column. Clues to the left of a row represent the sum of any UNSHADED cells between the 1 and 9 in that row.
1957: Normal 6x6 sudoku rules apply. (Place the digits 1 to 6, once each, in every row, column and region). Yin Yang: Shade some cells such that all shaded cells form one orthogonally connected area, as do all unshaded cells, and no 2x2 area is entirely shaded or unshaded. Counting Yin Yang: A digit in a shaded cell shows how many times that digit appears in shaded cells. Quadruples: A digit in a circle must appear in the surrounding 4 cells. If a digit appears twice in a circle, it must appear twice in the surrounding 4 cells.
1958: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along the orange line must be broken into one or more contiguous groups of cells that each sum to ten. Such groups cannot overlap. Digits may repeat within such sums if allowed by other rules. For example, 513173 is a valid fill for a length 6 line, because it can be broken into 5131 and 73, each of which sum to 10. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle.
1959: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along a green line have a difference of at least five. Box borders divide a blue line into segments with the same sum. Digits on the purple line must be a consecutive set of digits, in any order.
1960: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in the circle. Digits in a cage sum to the given total. A purple line contains a series of consecutive digits in any order. Identical digits cannot appear in the same position within any two 3x3 boxes.
1961: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits may not repeat within a cage, and sum to the number shown. The digits along each arrow must sum to the digit in the circled cell. Digits separated by a white dot must be consecutive.
1962: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along any individual line, each line segment within a different 3x3 box must sum to the same total. Different lines may have different totals. Additionally, along ALL these same lines, digits an equal distance from the centre of the line sum to the same total. For odd length lines, the total is the digit in the centre of the line. (In other words, the lines in this puzzle are simultaneously 'region sum' and 'zipper' lines.)
1963: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cells a knight's move apart in chess must not be the same digit. Any 2x2 area of cells in the grid must contain at least one digit from each modulo 3 set: 147, 258, 369. Digits in cells separated by a black dot must be in a 1:2 ratio. Digits along a thermometer must increase from the bulb end.
1964: Normal sudoku rules apply. Box borders divide each line into segments with the same sum. Digits in a cage sum to the number in the top left corner of that cage. One digit is double the other in cells separated by a black dot.
1965: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. A purple line contains a set of consecutive digits, in any order. Adjacent digits on a green line must have a difference of at least five. Any set of three adjacent digits on an orange line must have one digit from each of the following sets: 123, 456, 789. Digits on a red line must have a value between the values of the digits in that line's circles. Box borders divide a blue line into segments with equal sums. Digits joined by an X sum to 10; digits joined by a V sum to 5. Digits joined by a white dot must be consecutive; digits joined by a black dot must be in a 2:1 ratio.
1966: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the digits from 1 to 9 into two teams such that every digit from 1 to 9 is in exactly one of the two teams. Thereby, the finished grid has areas (of orthogonally connected cells) which contain only digits from one team and are bounded by digits of the other team and/or the border of the grid. A number clue gives the sum of all the digits in such an area. Digits may repeat in such an area and the sum clues are in an arbitrary position within the area. Each area has at most one clue, but may also have none at all.
1967: Normal sudoku rules apply. Numbers inside a circle indicate the sum of the digits in the four cells covered by the corresponding circle, which may include repeat digits. Each purple line contains a set of consecutive digits, in any order, without repeats.
1968: Normal sudoku rules apply. Nine cells (one per row/column/box) are doublers, and have values equal to double their digit. Each digit appears in exactly one doubler. A value X in a cage points to a second value Y located X cells away vertically or horizontally. The number in the top left corner of the cage indicates the sum of X+Y.
1969: Place the digits 0 to 8 once each in every row, column and 3x3 box. One cell in every row, column and box is a “doubler”. This cell counts as double its value for the rules below. Each of the digits 0 to 8 appears exactly once in a doubler cell. Values on an X sum to 10. Values on a V sum to 5. Digits in a cage may not repeat. Values in a cage sum to the total in the top-left most corner of the cage. The grid is partially covered in fog. Placing correct digits will clear the fog from surrounding cells. Guessing is not necessary.
1970: Normal sudoku rules apply. Box borders divide blue lines into segments with equal sums. Digits on a gold line do not repeat and are not consecutive with any other digits on the line.
1971: Fill the grid with eight non-overlapping 2x4 regions oriented horizontally (i.e. 2 rows and 4 columns), such that each region contains the digits from 1 to 8 once each and no digit repeats in any row or column. Cells outside regions don't contain digits. Draw a single one-cell-wide loop in the grid that travels orthogonally, doesn't branch, and isn't allowed to touch itself, not even diagonally, and doesn't pass through any of the empty cells. Any two adjacent cells along this loop must include one extreme digit [1,2,7,8] and one medium digit [3,4,5,6]. For each region N, the digit N must be on the loop within this region. (Regions are numbered in reading order, based on the position of their top left cell, i.e. a region with its top left cell further down in the grid than another region will have the higher region number. If two regions have their top left cell in the same row, the region on the right will have the higher region number.) Digits along marked diagonals sum to the number indicated outside the grid.
1972: Normal sudoku rules apply. "V" can be either "inequality" (arrow ‘points’ to smaller digit) or "two digits sum to 5" or both. If the two digits do sum to 5, the "V" can be in any orientation and does not necessarily indicate ‘greater than/less than’. Digits must not repeat in cells that are a chess knight's move apart. The digits in a cage must sum to the number printed in its corner. Entering a correct digit will clear the fog from around that cell.
1973: Place the digits from 1 to 6 exactly once in every row, column, and region. The regions are orthogonally OR diagonally connected and must be located by the solver. A number in the top left corner of a cell indicates the sum of the digits in the orthogonally connected section of the region that cell belongs to. A cell with a red X in the bottom right corner indicates the size (ie the number of cells) of the orthogonally connected section of the region that cell belongs to. All possible size clues (red Xs) are given.
1974: Normal sudoku rules apply. Cells touching diagonally cannot contain the same digit. Lines in the grid act as both Region Sum Lines and Parity Lines. Along a Region Sum Line, box borders divide the line into segments with equal totals. Different lines may have different totals. Along a Parity Line, digits must alternate between even and odd values.
1975: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits an equal distance from the circled centre of a lavender zipper line sum to the central digit.
1976: Normal sudoku rules apply. The sum of digits on an arrow must equal one of the digits in the four cells surrounding the connected circle. If more than one arrow on the same circle has the same sum, then said sum must appear at least that many times in the cells surrounding the circle.
1977: Place the digits 0 to 8 in each row, column and box. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Digits on an X sum to 10. Digits on a V sum to 5. Digits on a white dot are consecutive.
1978: Normal sudoku rules apply. Enter correct digits to clear fog. No guessing is necessary. In every row, column and box, there is exactly one 'pseudo cell'. The digits 1-9 each appear once in a pseudo cell. The real value of a pseudo cell is calculated by adding its row number to its column number. Eg: if there is a pseudo cell in r8c5, it has the value of 13, regardless of which digit is in that cell. On a lavender 'zipper' line, the values of any pair of cells that are an equal distance from the central spot always sum to the value on that central spot. On a turquoise 'same difference' line, the values of adjacent cells always have the same difference (but this difference may be different for different turquoise lines.) Values joined by a V sum to 5.
1979: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade an orthogonally connected group of cells within each dashed cage. Two shaded cells may not share a cage border. No two orthogonally touching cages may contain the same number of shaded cells. Circles are unshaded and contain the count of shaded cells in their cage. Values in the top left of cages (if given) sum the digits in shaded cells in the cage. Digits may not repeat in shaded cells in the cage (no restriction on unshaded cells). Digits in cells joined by a black dot are in a 2:1 ratio.
1980: Each row and column contains the digits from 1 to 6 once each. The digits in each cage sum to a prime number but no two cages sum to the same prime. Digits in a cage MAY repeat.
1981: Normal sudoku rules apply. For every coloured cell, the digits in all orthogonal neighbours (ie those sharing an edge with that cell) are either all greater or all less than the digit in the cell. A digit cannot repeat along a main diagonal (marked in green).
1982: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow must sum to the digit in that arrow’s circle. A border square is a 2x2 square that crosses at least one box border. For all border squares except for the four marked in grey, its two diagonals sum to the same number. The diagonals of different border squares may sum to different numbers.
1983: Normal sudoku rules apply. Values along a purple line comprise a set of non-repeating, consecutive numbers (in any order). A black dot joins two values in a 1:2 ratio.
1984: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on a line must form a valid chess move by the indicated piece on a 3x3 numpad. For example, a 1 on a knight line may only have the numbers 6 and 8 next to it so 6-1-8-1 would be valid. Pawns can only move exactly one cell up or one cell down, so 2-5-8-5 would be a valid pawn line.
1985: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along an orange line have a difference of at least four. Box borders break a blue line into segments with the same sum. Digits inside a cage do not repeat and sum to the total indicated.
1986: Normal sudoku rules apply. Placing a correct digit will clear the fog from the neighbouring cells. Guessing is not required. Lines travel orthogonally or diagonally through the centres of cells. They do not branch and do not cross themselves or each other. All given lines are a different colour. A grey dot may hide part of a line. Lines are “region-subset lines” ie The 3x3 box borders divide lines into segments. If a digit appears in a segment of length N, it must appear in all segments of length N or greater on that line. All lines have at least two segments. In addition, a digit on a line indicates the number of times that digit appears on that line.
1987: Normal sudoku rules apply. Each cell is either land or water. All cells of the same type must be orthogonally connected. No 2x2 area may be entirely land or entirely water. Line Types: - Renban (pink) - Digits on a pink line don't repeat, and form a consecutive sequence, but these can be arranged in any order along the line. - Nabner (yellow) - A digit on a yellow line cannot be consecutive with (or the same as) any other digit anywhere on the line. - German Whisper (green) - Adjacent digits on a green line must have a difference of at least 5. - Region Sum (blue) - Digits along a blue line must have the same total within each 3x3 box. - Parity (red) - Digits along a red line must alternate between odd and even. - Entropic (orange) - Any group of 3 adjacent digits on an orange line must contain a low digit (1, 2 or 3), a medium digit (4, 5 or 6), and a high digit (7, 8 or 9). - Palindrome (grey) - A grey line must read the same in either direction. - Same Difference (turquoise) - Each pair of adjacent digits along a turquoise line must have the same difference. ZIPPERY WHEN WET: • Any line that is completely wet (only enters water cells) loses the property of its presenting colour, and instead becomes a zipper line. Along a zipper line, each pair of digits that are the same distance from the line's central cell, sum to the digit in that centre cell. • Any line that is completely dry (only enters land cells) behaves normally, as described in the list above. It does not behave like a zipper line. • If a line is partly dry and partly wet, it retains its presenting property, but it is ALSO a zipper line as well.
1988: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Correctly entered digits remove fog in surrounding cells. Cells with a grey square contain an even digit. Each line has a distinct color. Lines do not branch or cross and only move orthogonally. All lines have a length of 3 or more. The box location of each line's ends determine its type(s): 1: Ten Line 2: Renban 3: German Whisper 4: Same Difference 5: Between 6: Modular 7: Nabner 8: Region Sum 9: Entropic e.g. yellow has one end at r3c5 and the other at r7c5. It is both Renban (box 2) and Region Sum (box 8). Ten Line: The line can be broken into segments such that each sums to 10. Renban: The line contains a set of non-repeating consecutive digits, in any order. German Whisper: Adjacent digits along this line must differ by at least 5. Same Difference: Adjacent digits along this line have the same difference for all pairs. Between: All other digits along the line have values that fall strictly between those of the ends. Modular: Every group of 3 consecutive cells along the line contains a full set of remainders modulo 3: one from (1,4,7), one from (2,5,8), and one from (3,6,9). Nabner: None of the digits on the line repeat, nor are consecutive with any other digit along the line. Region Sum: Box borders break the line into segments with the same sum. Entropic: Every group of 3 consecutive cells along the line must contain a low (1,2,3), mid (4,5,6), and high (7,8,9) digit.
1989: Bilbo Bobbins is on a quest to, uh, "procure" the Arkenstone (R5C5) that sits in Dragon Snyder's Lair (a 2x2 region in box 5) under Logic Mountain. R9C1 marks the entrance to the Whispering Tunnels: an orthogonally connected region leading to the lair. Adjacent digits along the tunnels (and deadends) differ by at least 5. The path from start to lair (ignoring deadends) is 26 cells. With Arkenstone acquired, Bilbo must escape through the Modular Passage, that begins on the opposite side of the lair and leads to a secret door exiting the mountain (R5C9). Every set of three digits along this passage (which does not branch) must contain one each from the sets {1,4,7}, {2,5,8}, and {3,6,9}. The total sum of digits along this "Secret" passage is 45. Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells ("walls") and leave others unshaded ("tunnels", "lair", "passage") such that no 2x2 region (except the lair) is fully shaded or unshaded. Also, there are no "checkerboard" patterns of shaded/unshaded cells, i.e. the unshaded region does not touch itself diagonally. All wall cells must be in orthogonally connected groups with at least one cell at the grid's edge. All caged cells are either tunnel or passage. The digit in the cage, plus its modifier, indicates how many unshaded cells (including itself) can be seen orthogonally from that position (walls block sight). E.g., if a cage contains a 7 and has a "-2" modifier, then that cell can "see" 5 unshaded cells total (including itself).
1990: Normal sudoku rules apply. Within a cage, digits sum to the total given.
1991: Draw a loop that moves orthogonally between cells and does not visit any cell more than once. Cells containing clues must not be visited by the loop. Every other unvisited cell (i.e. those that do not contain clues) must belong to a pentomino - areas of five orthogonally connected cells. No pentomino shape may repeat and they must not touch each other, not even diagonally. (A rotation or reflection of a pentomino should be treated as a repeat of that pentomino and therefore not allowed.) Not all of the 12 possible pentomino shapes are necessarily used. A clue specifies the number of cells belonging to pentominoes in the indicated direction. To make the "answer check" function work, enter the digit 8 in every cell that contains a pentomino.
1992: Normal sudoku rules apply. Divide the grid into yellow regions and brown regions. Each region must consist of orthogonally connected cells, and two regions of the same colour may not share an orthogonal edge. Brown regions (chocolate bars) must be rectangular or square. Yellows regions (bananas) must NOT be square / rectangular. Digits may repeat within regions. A digit in a banana cell indicates exactly how many banana cells contain that digit. A digit in a brown diamond belongs to a chocolate bar and indicates the size of that chocolate bar. Every chocolate bar has a different size. A digit on an arrow cell indicates the total sum of the closest (neighbouring) cells in each of the indicated directions.
1993: Place the same 4-digit subset from the digits 1 – 9 in each row, column and 2 x 2 box. Digits along a thermometer must increase from the bulb end. Digits separated by the black dot have a 2 to 1 ratio. Digits separated by the white dot are consecutive. The BLUE square contains an even number. (I know the card calls it a grey square - sorry)
1994: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits on a grey line (including the hook) differ by exactly N, where N is the digit on the corresponding fish.
1995: Place the digits 1-7 exactly once in every row and column. Place 8 polyominoes (an L pentomino, an N pentomino, a P pentomino, a U pentomino, a V pentomino, a Y pentomino, a Z pentomino and a 2x3 rectangle) exactly once in such a way that only the cells with grey text in them are not covered by one of the shapes (ie the "8", the "Jun" and 6 cells with "X" in them), so the grid spells out 8 June (Simon's Birthday). The polyominoes can be reflected and rotated as required. Each cage is part of a polyomino and no polyomino can have more than one cage. This cage can be anywhere in the polyomino. The small number in the top left of the cage gives the sum of the digits of that polyomino and digits can't repeat within a polyomino. The digits along the pointed diagonal sum to 45. There are some cells with oddballs in the puzzle, which have odd digits in it. These are put in, because Simon is a bit of an oddball, in the most positive way: an eccentric and exceptional character.
1996: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along an orange line have a difference of at least four. Cells separated by a "6 ball” sum to six.
1997: Normal sudoku rules apply. The circled cell contains an odd digit. Divide each grey line into at least two non-overlapping segments. The digits on each segment of a line sum to the same total. (Different lines may have different totals.) Additionally each segment individually forms a set of non-repeating consecutive digits in any order.
1998: Normal sudoku rules apply. The 3x3 box borders divide a blue line into segments. The sum of the digits along each segment is the same for that line. Different lines may have different segment sums. Eg r4c7+r4c8 = r1c6+r2c6+r3c6 = r1c7+r2c8+r3c9+r3c8
1999: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a thermometer, digits increase from the bulb to the tip.
2000: 1-9 must be placed in each row, column and marked region. Purple lines contain a set of non-repeating consecutive numbers in any order. Along the thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end. Digits along an arrow sum to the circled digit.
2001: Normal sudoku rules apply. The grid is covered in fog. Placing correct digits reveals clues in the surrounding 3x3 area. No guessing is required. Shade some cells so that all shaded cells are orthogonally connected and all unshaded cells are orthogonally connected. No 2x2 area can be completely shaded or unshaded. The value of a shaded cell is the sum of its row number and its column number. The value of an unshaded cell is its digit. Values an equal distance to the circled cente of a line sum to the central value. All lines are of odd length, only move orthogonally and don't share cells with other lines.
2002: Solvers must determine a set of nine digits from 1 to 9 (inclusive), WHICH MAY INCLUDE REPEATS. Place one of these digits into each uncoloured cell such that every row and column with less than nine cells contains a subset of these nine digits and each marked region and 9-cell row/column contains all of these nine digits. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in the connected circle. Squares contain even digits; and white dots separate consecutive digits. For clarity, the coloured cells are decorative and contain NO digits.
2003: Normal sudoku rules apply. AIM OF EXPERIMENT: Finkz the rat must reach the cupcake by finding a path through the maze. The path will be a snaking line that passes through the centres of cells, without visiting any cell more than once, crossing itself or passing through any thick maze walls. As well as moving orthogonally, Finkz may move diagonally if there's a 2x2 space in which to do so, but may never pass diagonally through the rounded end / corner of a wall. TEST CONSTRAINT: In this experiment, any two adjacent cells along the correct path must sum to a prime number. Also, ALL digits within a marked 3x2 sudoku box that lie anywhere on the correct path must sum to a prime number too.
2004: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle.
2005: Fill the grid with the digits 0-9 so that digits do not repeat in a row, column, or 3x3 box, and exactly one cell in each row, column, and box contains two digits. A cell's value is equal to the sum of its digits. A cage's product is equal to the value of each of its cells multiplied together. Each cage's product is consecutive with that of exactly one other cage in the puzzle, and no two cages have the same product. Some cage products are given, others must be deduced. Digits cannot repeat within a cage (but values can). The sum of the values along an arrow is equal to the value in the connected circle. Values in cells with a shaded square must be even.
2006: Normal sudoku rules apply. No digit repeats along a marked diagonal. Digits in cages sum to the indicated value. Digits on a purple line (each ‘line’ in this puzzle contains 5 cells) form a set of consecutive digits in any order. Digits in cells connected by "X" sum to 10.
2007: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits on an arrow sum to the digit in that arrow's circle. Arrows do not branch, cross or share cells (including circles) with other arrows. A digit in a circle gives how many times that digit appears in circles. Arrow circles count as circles for this rule. The grid is partially covered in fog. Entering a correct digit in the grid will clear the fog around that digit. No guessing is required.
2008: Normal 8x8 sudoku rules apply; fill the grid with the digits 1-8 so that no digit repeats in a row, column, or marked 4x2 box. AIM OF EXPERIMENT: Finkz the rat must reach the cupcake by finding a path through the maze. The path will be a snaking line that passes through the centres of cells, without visiting any cell more than once, crossing itself or passing through any thick maze walls. As well as moving orthogonally, Finkz may move diagonally if there's a 2x2 space in which to do so, but may never pass diagonally through the rounded end / corner of a wall. TEST CONSTRAINT: In this experiment, any two adjacent cells along the correct path must sum to at least ten.
2009: The puzzle uses killer, sandwich and thermo rules: All coloured 'cages' sum to 19, clues outside the grid show the sum of digits between the 1 and the 9 in that row/column, and thermometers have numbers strictly increasing from the 'bulb'.
2010: Normal sudoku rules apply. In addition each thermo must either freeze or increase from the bulb. The clues outside the grid give the sum of the cells between 1 and 9.
2011: Normal Sudoku rules apply. In addition, each thermometer must strictly increase along its length from the bulb.
2012: Normal sudoku rules apply, and digits increase along thermometers from the bulb. Each thermo shown (the three passing through the centre are straight lines) has a bulb at one end, though for some of them that bulb is not shown.
2013: Normal sudoku rules apply. Colour the x'th cell in each row red (where x is the digit in column 1 of that row) and colour the y'th cell in each column blue (where y is the digit in row 1 of that column). Every row, column and box must contain exactly one red and one blue cell, and red and blue cells may not overlap. Clues outside the grid indicate the sum of digits sandwiched between the red and blue cell in that row/column.
2014: Normal sudoku rules apply. Shade some cells (walls) such that they form orthogonally connected regions that must touch an edge of the grid. Similarly, leave some cells unshaded (tunnel) to form a single orthogonally connected path, which may not touch itself diagonally and does not branch. No 2x2 area of the grid may be completely shaded or unshaded. Cells marked with a square indicate how many cells (including themselves) they see orthogonally (walls block their view, but they may themselves be walls). White dots indicate consecutive digits along the path (all white dots are shown). Black dots indicate that cells are in a 1:2 ratio within the wall (all black dots are shown). Note that dots do not disclose relationships between shaded and unshaded cells.
2015: Normal sudoku rules apply. Within a 3x3 box, cells a single knight's move apart (in chess) cannot contain consecutive digits.
2016: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage sum to the number given. The sum of the digits along an arrow is equal to the digit in the connected circle.
2017: Normal sudoku rules apply. No two cells which share an edge may contain digits adding to 5 or 10. Along a thermometer, digits must increase from the bulb end. Digits in a cage may not repeat, and they must sum to the given total. Digits in the green bowtie shape celebrate 600,000 subscribers, in that the digits appearing in that area multiply to 600,000.
2018: Place the digits 0-8 in the grid such that no digit repeats in a row, column or box. Along green lines, adjacent digits differ by at least 5. A digit in a circle indicates the number of circles containing that digit.
2019: Normal sudoku rules apply. Adjacent digits along the centipede differ by at least 5. A digit on a mushroom indicates how many mushrooms contain that digit. White dots separate consecutive digits. Digits on the pink cannon form a non-repeating consecutive sequence.
2020: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in a cage must sum to the number in the corner of the cage Digits separated by a black dot have a 1:2 ratio. Digits separated by a white dot are consecutive. Digits a 'knight’s move' apart cannot sum to 5 or 15.
2021: Normal sudoku rules apply. Placing correct digits will remove fog from surrounding cells to reveal more clues. Somewhere in the fog are 9 marked cells - one in every row, column and 3x3 box. These cells must contain the digits 1-9 once each. For each marked cell, the sum of ALL the digits in the cells up to and including that marked cell, (top to bottom, left to right, as one might read) must always sum to a square number.
2022: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits in cages do not repeat and sum to the number indicated.
2023: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along thermometers increase from the bulb end. Digits do not repeat along the indicated diagonal.
2024: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits along a thermometer increase from the bulb end.
2025: Normal sudoku rules apply.\n\nSkyscraper: Each digit should be viewed as a skyscraper with height equal to its value. Clues outside the grid indicate how many digits are 'seen' along that diagonal, with higher digits blocking lower or identical digits from view.
2026: Normal sudoku rules apply. Along a thermometer, digits increase from the bulb end.
2027: Normal 6x6 sudoku rules apply. (Place the digits 1 to 6, once each, in every row, column and outlined box). Boxes are numbered in normal reading order. Orthogonally adjacent digits must not sum to their box number(s). For example, r2c4 and r3c4 must not sum to 2 or 4. Additionally, diagonally adjacent digits within the same box must not sum to their box number. The inequality sign points to the lower digit.
2028: Normal sudoku rules apply. Digits do not repeat along a marked blue diagonal. A diamond shows that there exist two digits N steps away from the diamond in an orthogonal direction that have a difference of N, where N is the digit in the diamond. Not all diamonds are necessarily given. (For example, if r6c4 is a 3, then at least one pair of digits from the set of digits in r3c4, r6c7, r9c4 and r6c1 must have a difference of 3).
2029: In each N-by-N grid, normal N-by-N Sudoku rules apply. Overlapping cells contain the same digit eg if r6c8 is a 4 in the 9x9 grid then it is also a 4 in r1c1 of the 6x6 grid. COUNTING CARDS: A digit in a cell with a suit symbol indicates how many times that digit appears in cells with that suit symbol. Eg if r6c5 of the 9x9 grid contains a 6 then exactly 6 diamond cells in the grid must contain a 6.
